comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Fidelity flag for the EP64 fixed-a2a line (the 17.55% / 20.558% runs above and the follow-ups in #7279): those runs route with QB balancing off — `qb_routing` defaults to False in `launch_cw_scale.py`, and the recorded submit commands never set `SCALE_MOE_QB`. Measured with an exact drop counter at the same operating point, that configuration router-collapses: routed experts drop 85–89% of assignments early in training and oscillate 17–79% over a full 120-step run. The always-on shared expert keeps loss descending, so the collapse is invisible in loss curves.

Two consequences for reading MFU numbers in that regime: dropped-assignment fraction is a fidelity metric those runs do not report, and heavy-drop runs read *higher* MFU (dropped assignments gather a zero pad row and do less real work), so QB-off vs QB-on MFU gaps are upper bounds. With QB on at the same shape: 22.60% p50 at cf1.0 (settles at ~6% drops) and 20.85% at cf1.15 (3.7% at step 119 and declining — the only measured config under the ~3% reference bar).

Full measurements, drop-metric validation, and repro knobs: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7279#issuecomment-5080435482. This flag covers only the EP64 fixed-a2a lineage; QB state for the other tracker rows is being audited separately.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 **EP64 with a custom scatter-add adjoint beats the best prior FSDP figure at both architectures we measured, and the fine-granularity result is compliant at 1.44% dropped assignments.**

Both results here are one-rack EP64 with the custom adjoint. The comparison column is the best previously reported FSDP figure for the same architecture, sourced per row below the table.

| architecture | this work (EP64, 1 rack) | drops | prior best (FSDP) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| d6144 · 4-of-128 · 48L | 24.594% | 9–13% | 23.1% |
| d6144 · 4-of-128, compliant (projected) | ~23.9% | ≤3% | 23.1% |
| d5120 · 8-of-256 · i1280 · 48L | **20.708%** | **1.44%** | 19.2% |
| d5120 · 8-of-256, at a 5% bar | 21.849% | 3.66% | 19.2% |

Sources for the comparison column: **23.1%** is the full-feature + host-offload d6144 4-of-128 result in https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7201#issuecomment-5036748495 (255.3K tok/s, one rack measured); **19.2%** is the "fine granularity" row of the "Measured architecture data points (GB200)" table in this issue's body (two-rack measurement). Details and caveats below.

## d5120 · 8-of-256 · i1280 — measured compliant

350-step legs on one allocation draw, drop fractions are true 100-step tails, QB-on, custom adjoint:

| spill m | capacity factor | p50 MFU | tail-100 drops |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 | 1.0 | 22.062% | 7.10% |
| 3 | 1.0 | 21.849% | 3.66% |
| 3 | 1.05 | 20.670% | 1.72% |
| **3** | **1.0625** | **20.708%** | **1.44%** |
| 0 | 1.15 | 20.416% | 2.60% |

Against the 19.2% figure: **+1.5pp while dropping under 1.5% of routed assignments**, or **+2.6pp at 3.66%** under a 5% bar.

The mechanism buying the fidelity is same-step spill — when a token's chosen expert bucket is full, the assignment is re-offered to the next-ranked expert *that token already selected* if that bucket has headroom, rather than dropped. Bucket layout, capacity and the fixed-capacity all-to-all are unchanged. It costs 0.213pp and halves drops, cheap for a structural reason: expert GEMMs run on capacity-sized buffers whether or not a slot is filled, so spill adds index work, never matmul work. Combining it with a small capacity increase beats buying capacity alone on both axes — 20.708% at 1.44% versus 20.416% at 2.60%.

## d6144 · 4-of-128 — the one-rack hero candidate

`/mwittmann/ep25d5-d6144-e128-bf16-120-0726-1140-v3`, 120/120 steps, 16/16 tasks: EP64 · batch 1024 · seq 4096 · QB-on · capacity factor 1.0 · host offload · default BFC allocator at the default 0.75 fraction · sliding window 2048. Steady tail (steps 90–119) p10 24.434 / p50 24.594 / p90 24.771, sd 0.118, 276.4K tok/s, 15.174 s/step, loss 10.31 → 5.59.

**Plan against ~23.9%, not 24.594%.** The raw figure is measured at 9–13% dropped assignments; applying the measured cost of capacity factor 1.05 plus spill (about −0.65pp) to reach a ≤3% bar still exceeds 23.1%. A run that drops more reads higher MFU, because dropped assignments gather a zero pad row and do less real work, so the raw number should not be compared to a low-drop configuration without that adjustment.

## Caveats

- **The drop fractions of both prior figures are unmeasured**, so both comparisons are one-sided on fidelity. Those runs compute a per-layer drop count but never emit it; the tracker-logging fix is one line and would settle it permanently for one job's cost. This is the largest uncertainty on both results.
- The 19.2% figure is a two-rack measurement while the 8-of-256 result here is one rack, so that comparison bundles parallelization, the adjoint and spill together rather than isolating a parallelization delta. The 23.1% d6144 figure is one rack, so that comparison is rack-matched.
- The 4-of-128 run uses sliding window 2048 where the 23.1% configuration uses 512 with 5:1 local:global, so it does **more** attention work; it also lacks XSA, the attention gate, and GatedNorm, which that configuration has. Both point the same way.
- The 8-of-256 drop figures are 350-step tails and the 4-of-128 figure is 120-step; they are not comparable to each other. The LR schedule is defined over `num_train_steps`, so a given step index sits at a different schedule position in runs of different lengths, and drops fall as the learning rate anneals.
- Capacity factor below 1.0 cannot help: total capacity is exactly `cf × total_assignments`, so drops are bounded below by `1 − cf` regardless of routing.

## Two inputs for choosing between candidates

**4-of-256 at EP64 does not fit one rack**, measured on all 16 tasks: 92.02 GiB resident plus a single 106.63 GiB temp arena against 184.3 GiB physical, so no memory fraction closes it. The resident set decomposes exactly into expert parameters, MuonH momentum and the replicated embedding trio — nothing is mis-sharded. Consistent with the 4-of-256 candidate command above, which already assumes two racks plus offload.

**Drop recovery is bounded by routing granularity.** Spill can only re-offer an assignment to an expert the token itself selected, so top-4 shapes have at most 3 attempts and saturate there — measured through the shipping kernel, the drop fraction is flat from m=3 through m=7 at 4-of-256, while 8-of-256 keeps improving from 2.73% to 1.57%. Top-4 also carries a higher statistical floor, since the per-bucket mean load halves. Neither top-4 candidate reaches a 3% bar by spill alone at capacity factor 1.0; they need capacity headroom on top, at roughly −0.58pp per +0.05.

Method, the full frontier including a falsified capacity-alignment hypothesis, and the reproduction knobs are in #7279.

comments.body:
🤖 **Receiver-ECHO · MuonH · d5120 · 4-of-256 experts · 48 layers — 394.8B total / ~13.0B active — one-rack EP64 BF16**

The 20-step EP64 screen completed on 16×4 GB200 GPUs with **24.153% median MFU**, **462,267 tokens/s**, and **9.073 s/step** over steps 5–19. The MFU uses the true GB200 BF16 dense denominator of 2.5 PFLOP/s per GPU. Mean exact aggregate post-ECHO assignment drop over the same window was **2.765%**; final loss was finite at **7.945**.

All 16 Iris tasks and 64 ranks completed 20/20 steps with zero failures, preemptions, or retries. This is a short performance screen, not a long-run stability or drop-rate qualification.

| Run | Median MFU | Median step | Median throughput | Mean assignment drop | Final loss |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Matched control | 22.374% | 9.795 s | 428,217 tok/s | 2.918% | 7.943 |
| Padded, stack-sharded non-expert Muon | 24.153% | 9.073 s | 462,267 tok/s | 2.765% | 7.945 |

<details>
<summary>Architecture, kernel path, semantics, validation, and reproduction</summary>

### Architecture

- 48 layers, hidden size 5,120
- 256 routed experts, top-4 routing
- routed expert intermediate size 2,048
- one shared expert with intermediate size 5,120
- global batch 1,024, sequence length 4,096, sliding window 512
- MuonH with SYRK; BF16 training
- EP64 on 16 nodes × 4 GB200 GPUs, one process per GPU
- 394,844,428,288 total parameters; approximately 13.0B active non-embedding parameters per token

### Kernel path

- FA4 CuTe attention
- fixed-shape BF16 token all-to-all
- receiver-pooled ECHO with same-expert clones, sparse clone weights, two padding experts, and at most ten receiver expert segments
- two sender-balanced pipeline chunks
- Sonic dispatch, slot gather, and combine
- SM100 grouped expert GEMMs and grouped weight gradients
- quantile balancing enabled
- XLA latency-hiding scheduler with collective-overlap limit 4
- CUDA command buffers enabled; PGLE disabled for the matched screen

### Receiver-ECHO and drop semantics

An accepted routed assignment executes the router-selected expert, either on its home shard or on a same-expert receiver clone. The path is not dropless: fixed receiver envelopes remain bounded, and assignments that exceed those envelopes are dropped. The reported 2.765% is the exact aggregate assignment drop after ECHO placement, averaged over steps 5–19; it is not a whole-token drop rate.

### Muon change

Five 48-layer non-expert Muon parameter stacks are zero-padded to 64 rows so the Newton–Schulz batch can shard across the 64-way expert mesh. The padded result is resharded directly to the original parameter layout before slicing, so the padded stack is not replicated on every device. Dummy rows remain zero and are removed before applying the update.

The implementation is in [`497423bc6`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/497423bc6716ad102fc53ebdebd7bfdb38304dcc). Local BF16 checks covered square and both rectangular matrix orientations and produced identical padded/unpadded updates. Repository tests also assert that the padded result returns with the original shape and sharding.

### Validation scope

- The matched rack A/B changed only `SCALE_MUON_PAD_NONEXPERT=0` to `1`.
- Both runs used `JAX_ENABLE_PGLE=false` and completed without Iris retries.
- The rack losses ended at 7.943 and 7.945 after 20 steps.
- No XProf/HLO capture was taken after enabling padded Muon; the available profile predates this optimizer change.

### Reproduction

From snapshot [`1a88e1f3b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/1a88e1f3be7c26673664922e409234226952a068), with `WANDB_API_KEY` set externally:

```bash
JAX_ENABLE_PGLE=false SCALE_MUON_PAD_NONEXPERT=1 \
  .agents/projects/7201-ep64-drop3/run_best_bf16_ep64.sh \
  ep30-cx-muon-pad-nopgle-20260727-0714 32536 20
```

The submission script is [permalinked here](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1a88e1f3be7c26673664922e409234226952a068/.agents/projects/7201-ep64-drop3/run_best_bf16_ep64.sh). The research branch is [`research/rav/7201-ep64-muon-pad`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/research/rav/7201-ep64-muon-pad).

### Run artifacts

- Padded Muon: [W&B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/rav_moe/runs/ep30-cx-muon-pad-nopgle-20260727-0714) · [Iris](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Frav%2Fep30-cx-muon-pad-nopgle-20260727-0714)
- Matched control: [W&B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/rav_moe/runs/ep30-cx-muon-control-nopgle-20260727-0714) · [Iris](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Frav%2Fep30-cx-muon-control-nopgle-20260727-0714)
- Append-only investigation log: [`7201-ep64-mfu.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1a88e1f3be7c26673664922e409234226952a068/.agents/logbooks/7201-ep64-mfu.md)

</details>

comments.body:
🤖 **Long-context sweep — final d6144 stack, seqlen 4k → 8k → 65k at constant ~4.19M tokens/step (1 rack)**

Same [final 1-rack option](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7201#issuecomment-5093392733) (d6144, 48L, hetero-KV 12/6, MTP-1× dense, MoE-chunks 2, sliding-window 512, global-every-6). Each run holds **tokens/step fixed at ~4.19M** by halving batch as seqlen grows, so this isolates the pure cost of longer sequences.

| seq | batch | seq/GPU | tok/s | vs 4k | reported MFU | **true MFU** | wandb |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4k | 1024 | 16 | 246 K | — | 22.24% | **20.6%** | [run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/d6144-het126-mlp1x-cond-ch2-v1) |
| 8k | 512 | 8 | 241.6 K | **−1.8%** | 23.75% | **20.3%** | [run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/gb200-d6144-64gpu-seq8k-b512-ch2-v1) |
| 65k | 64 | 1 | 160.7 K | **−35%** | 36.45% | **17.0%** | [run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/gb200-d6144-64gpu-seq65k-b64-ch2-v1) |

**Findings**
- **8k context is nearly free**: −1.8% tok/s, true efficiency flat (~20.4%). Sliding-window 512 means the 40 local layers don't grow — only the 8 global layers pay more.
- **65k costs −35% tok/s** and true efficiency drops to **17%** (the 8 global layers do genuine 65k² attention + 1-seq/GPU parallelism hurts utilization). It **fits** — FA4 + sliding-window keeps 65k in HBM, no OOM.
- **The reported MFU is misleading and gets worse with seqlen.** `lm_flops_per_token` is window-blind: it counts full O(seq²) attention on *all* 48 layers, but 40 are windowed to 512. That overcounts FLOPs by **×1.08 at 4k, ×1.17 at 8k, ×2.14 at 65k** — so reported MFU *rises* (22→24→36) while true efficiency actually *falls* (20.6→20.3→17.0). Trust tok/s; treat MFU as inflated whenever seqlen ≠ 4k. Fix is a window-aware attention term (`min(seq, window)` on local layers, full on global).

```bash

  -e SCALE_HIDDEN_DIM 6144 -e SCALE_NUM_LAYERS 48 -e SCALE_NUM_HEADS 48 -e SCALE_NUM_KV_HEADS 12 \
  -e SCALE_LOCAL_KV_HEADS 12 -e SCALE_GLOBAL_KV_HEADS 6 \
  -e SCALE_NUM_EXPERTS 128 -e SCALE_TOP_K 4 -e SCALE_NUM_SHARED_EXPERTS 2 \
  -e SCALE_SEQ_LEN "$SEQ" -e SCALE_SLIDING_WINDOW 512 -e SCALE_GLOBAL_EVERY 6 -e SCALE_BATCH "$BATCH" -e SCALE_STEPS 25 \
  -e SCALE_DISABLE_LONG_ROPE 1 -e SCALE_ROPE_FRACTION 0.5 -e SCALE_ROPE_FUSED 1 \
  -e SCALE_MTP_DEPTH 1 -e SCALE_MTP_DENSE 1 -e SCALE_MTP_INTERMEDIATE 6144 \
  -e SCALE_DATA slimpajama -e SCALE_OPTIMIZER muonh \
  -e SCALE_MOE_QB 1 -e SCALE_XSA 1 -e SCALE_ATTN_GATE 1 -e SCALE_GATED_NORM 1 -e SCALE_OFFLOAD_OPT_STATE 1 -e SCALE_DISABLE_CHECKPOINT 1 \

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
Main thoughts on above comment-
going from 48 heads to 64 heads only drops tps from 262k to 243k, a 7% drop. This is a bit of a sweep spot in that this doesn't increase our parameter count by much due to kv cache (1-2B params total sharded over 64 gpus), doesn't increase MFU much due to efficiency of FA4, and doesn't increase saved activation memory at all. Will test quality later, but I expect it to help quality by more than 7%. This is also the same ratio used by Inkling. We can't expand MoE in the same way without hitting OOM pressure. If it were possible to fit more total expert parameters on a single rack that would be great. It is definitely possible in theory but I haven't found it. Increasing active experts while not increasing total experts will likely have limited gains. Our sparsity rate is also not that high, so would rather go sparser than less sparse.

Sliding window impact seems noisy. Sometimes 2048 runs faster than 1024. Will do more quality tests here. conv will likely get included.

Other thing to note here is that 256e / top-8 / routed-1536 (= same total params) is viable, for a 7% tps hit. Potentially worth it, will be close. Didn't test changing MoE chunk count here.

Our watch step is killing mean MFU, it runs at like 2 MFU. This job has watch every 20. Ideally we could make that step faster. I don't understand why its so slow. If not, watch every 40 might be worth it. Though it may cause us to miss some gradient spikes.

comments.body:
This issue has gone un-updated a while so wanted to add in a summary

August 2 — EP64 becomes competitive. On the then-current d5120 hero, the optimization ladder went from ragged EP64 at 260k tok/s / 15.0% median MFU, through fixed-capacity dispatch at 315k / 19.4%, gather dispatch at 360k / 21.9%, and structured custom VJPs at 389k / 24.1%. The selected stack sustained 383k tok/s / 23.7% median MFU over 200 steps. [Final 200-step result](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7279#issuecomment-5155747793)

August 5 — matched EP beats FSDP. On the same d6144, 4-of-128 shape and one rack, EP64 reached 316k tok/s / 27.8% median MFU, versus FSDP’s 235k / 19.4%. EP was doing less work because it dropped about 10% of assignments; correcting for that still left it around 25.5% MFU, roughly six points ahead. [Matched comparison](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7279#issuecomment-5167162893)

August 7–8 — FSDP optimization sweep adds about 9%. Small-parameter sharding plus pre-gather gate/up interleaving took the one-rack FSDP hero from 19.37% to 21.30% MFU, a replicated 7.9–9.1% throughput gain. The best measured step was 16.43 seconds, about 255k tok/s. Much of the gain later shrank after the one-process-per-GPU merge increased peak memory, so this is an optimization milestone rather than the current production number. [Sweep conclusion](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8054#issuecomment-5223621862)

August 8 — first strong d6144 LatentMoE candidate. The d6144, 4-of-192, i6272 EP64 candidate measured 262,396 tok/s on one rack, with 546B total and roughly 25B active parameters. This became the main EP/FSDP decision candidate. [Candidate comparison](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8062#issuecomment-5227823324)

August 14 — current 8-of-384 hero establishes its accepted baseline. The selected three-stripe fixed EP layout sustained 256,818 tok/s / 24.03% median MFU over steps 150–199 of a 200-step run, with 2.41% median drops. This is the most relevant current-shape reference; earlier raw tok/s records are not directly comparable. [Selected 8-of-384 result](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7279#issuecomment-5294194777)

August 16 — stock ragged EP gains 1.62 MFU points on the current hero. QuACK tile, persistence, and per-call-site cluster tuning moved the full 8-of-384 EP64 shape from 223k tok/s / 20.20% MFU to 241,116 tok/s / 21.82% MFU, with zero drops and unchanged loss. Follow-up work established that this path tops out near 22% because transport competes with expert GEMMs for SMs. [Tuning result](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8317#issuecomment-5308322722), [final ceiling](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8317#issuecomment-5313789958)

August 16–17 — fused Marin EP reaches 247k tok/s. On the older 4-of-192 shape, fused transport plus Pallas Blackwell ragged-dot expert GEMMs improved the step from about 18.1 to 17.0 seconds, or roughly 247k tok/s / 22.6% MFU, at 0.5–0.6% drops. Strategically important, but not directly comparable to the selected 8-of-384 hero. [Marin EP tracker](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8311)

August 17 — current hero reaches 25.3% MFU at node scale. The 8-of-384 shape ran on four GB200s at 47.4–48.4k tok/s / 25.08–25.56% MFU, with zero drops after step 19. This validates the compute path and shows top-8 itself does not reduce MFU, but it is not an EP64/rack throughput result; the rack-scale transport remains blocked. [Node-scale result](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8108#issuecomment-5312955273)

issues.title: GB200 Architecture TPS Tracker

issues.author: ravwojdyla-agent
issues.body:
## TL;DR

The Data Belay judge merged in #11019 gives signal on the 176 Datakit sources. Every test fixed in advance passes, except two inconclusive results: T7 for the knowledge group at d768, and T3's verdict agreement at d1024 (79% against an 80% bar). Null arms and dilution references read `no gain` at every rung. 12 of 12 retests on new seeds give the same verdict. Gain Δ correlates at r = 0.84 to 0.99 between two model families and between rungs. Math sources gain on math, code on code, English web on commonsense, and none of the 16 multilingual, 10 legal or 9 safety sources reads yes. Four weaknesses remain: at d1024, calls near the 1% floor depend on which 3 seeds ran; the knowledge group and CruxEval-O sit near noise; the harm check is underpowered at 3 seeds; and the run-on rule sends sources to d1024 that cannot end as a yes. The sweep is done (2026-11-17 09:30 UTC): 49 of 176 sources end yes, 21 mixed and 106 no. The final d1024 numbers and the list of yes sources are in [this comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11582#issuecomment-6944197467).

## Description

Data Belay judges a candidate dataset by training at a 20% share of the base mix and comparing answer loss on 6 eval groups (Paloma, Uncheatable, knowledge, commonsense, math, code) against two baselines. The gain is measured against a control that trains on the base mix alone. The harm is measured against 4 dilution references, which put the same 20% share into text that no eval measures (Japanese ClimbLab, Chinese, Thai and Arabic FinePDFs). Gain Δ is the relative change in a group's loss against the control, so negative is better. A group is `better` when its interval is below 0 and Δ is at least 1% in size (the 1% floor). It is `worse` when its harm interval is above the group's harm limit, which is the larger of 1% and 2.5 control seed SDs, computed from the d512 controls and used at every rung. Verdicts per rung are `helps`, `trade-off` (a better group and a group whose harm is unresolved), `no gain` and `hurts`. A yes is `helps` or `trade-off`.

Each source climbs a ladder of rungs (d512, d768, d1024) and stops after no at two consecutive rungs. One exception, the run-on rule: after two no's, a source still climbs if some group's Δ at the second rung is below 0. At the top rung, a source ends `yes` when d768 and d1024 both say yes, and `mixed` when they disagree. The judge is `experiments/data_belay/judge.py`.

Two models: "main's model" is the dense fast-track model on the main branch (`h100_ladder_model`), and "vanilla" is the vanilla Grug model, which ran the same sweep earlier.

Setup: main's model, one 8×H100 node per run on cw-us-east-02a at batch priority, 3 seeds per arm.

| Rung | Active params | Tokens | Median training time |
|---|---|---|---|
| d512 | 18M | 362M | 4.0 min |
| d768 | 53M | 1.07B | 12.3 min |
| d1024 | 145M | 2.89B | 45.5 min |

The candidates are the 176 Datakit caches at 20% that are not references. Three small sources prepared at 5 to 15% are left out because no references exist at those shares (#11481). Vanilla gives a second model family for replication (T3).

## Hypothesis or Goal

The tests and their pass and fail thresholds were written before the first run (2026-11-14 12:05 UTC):

- T1 Null calibration: extra control seeds judged as a candidate against control seeds 0-2 read `no gain`.
- T2 References: each reference judged against the other three reads `no gain`.
- T3 Cross-model replication: per group, gain Δ on main's model and vanilla correlate at r ≥ 0.8, and yes/no verdicts agree for ≥ 80% of sources. Fails at r < 0.5 or agreement < 70%.
- T4 Test-retest: 12 sources on seeds 3 to 5 agree on yes/no for ≥ 10 of 12. Fails below 8.
- T5 Rung consistency: per group, d512 and d768 gain Δ correlate at r ≥ 0.7. Fails below 0.4.
- T6 Face validity: math sources better on math, code sources on code, non-English sources `no gain` like the references.
- T7 Signal over noise: a group's SD of Δ across sources is ≥ 3× the Δ noise between two 3-seed arms of the same data. Fails below 1.5×; in between is inconclusive.

## Status

d512: 176 sources judged. d768: 176 judged (20 `helps`, 42 `trade-off`, 114 `no gain`). No source reads `hurts`. d1024: 87 judged (23 `helps`, 21 `trade-off`, 43 `no gain`; 85 also on vanilla). 19 are counted as two-rung ladders: their cache is too small for d1024's 2.89B tokens without repeating it more than 4 epochs, which `train` refuses. The other 70 stopped at d768. Final answers: 49 yes, 21 mixed, 106 no. The tables below were computed with 78 d1024 sources; the comment linked in the TL;DR has the final d1024 numbers, which change T3's d1024 agreement to 79%.

| Test | Result | Pass? |
|---|---|---|
| T1 | 4 null arms (control seeds 6-8, 9-11 and 12-14 at d512; 3-5 at d768): all `no gain` | yes |
| T2 | 4 of 4 references `no gain` at d512, d768 and d1024 | yes |
| T3 | Pearson r per group: d512 0.84-0.97 (175 sources), d768 0.87-0.98 (176), d1024 0.92-0.99 (85). Yes/no agreement: 89%, 97%, 79% | yes at d512 and d768; inconclusive at d1024 |
| T4 | 12 of 12 retests give the same verdict | yes |
| T5 | d512 vs d768 r = 0.89 (knowledge) to 0.99 (math). d768 vs d1024 r = 0.90 to 0.99 | yes |
| T6 | Yes at d768, with the median Δ over the category's sources: math 9 of 10 (math −7.7%), code 10 of 18 (code −3.3%), English web 13 of 16 (commonsense −2.3%), agent traces 15 of 46 (12 better on code). Multilingual 0 of 16, legal 0 of 10, safety 0 of 9, bio 0 of 5 | yes |
| T7 | Spread over noise on main's model, d512 / d768: Paloma 8.4× / 7.8×, Uncheatable 5.8× / 5.9×, knowledge 4.7× / 2.1×, commonsense 4.3× / 4.2×, math 9.6× / 6.7×, code 6.5× / 3.4× | yes, except knowledge at d768 (inconclusive) |

Sources that do not match an eval group read `no gain` with groups 0.5 to 4% worse than the control. That cost is the 20% share they take from the base mix, and the dilution references show the same cost, so the judge does not count it as harm.

### Where the method is weak

1. At d1024 the two models' yes/no verdicts differ for 15 of 76 sources, almost all near the 1% floor. 24 groups are `better` only on vanilla and 4 only on main's model. The effects are similar: in those 24 groups, the median Δ is −1.76% on vanilla and −1.18% on main's model. The intervals differ more: their median half-width is 1.29% on vanilla and 2.15% on main's model. Each model's flips fall in the groups where its own 3 d1024 control seeds varied more. Main's model's control varies more on knowledge (CV 0.99% vs 0.52%), commonsense (0.60% vs 0.32%) and code (0.34% vs 0.15%). Vanilla's varies more on math (1.21% vs 0.58%), and 3 of the 4 groups better only on main's model are math. With 3 seeds, a gain of 1 to 2% at d1024 is decided by noise in the estimated spread.
2. Knowledge and CruxEval-O sit near noise. Knowledge is 2.1× at d768. Per task on vanilla d512, CruxEval-O is 1.4×, TriviaQA 1.6× and the MMLU-Pro choice loss 2.2×, against HumanEval+ 6.8× and GSM8K 6.1×. Two code sources that read `helps` on vanilla and `no gain` on main's model improve HumanEval+ and MBPP+ on both models; CruxEval-O pulls the code group's mean toward 0 on main's model.
3. The harm check is underpowered. The median harm-interval half-width is about equal to the harm limit (vanilla d512: Paloma 0.87% against a 1.00% limit). 63 of 71 unresolved groups behind d512 trade-offs had a harm Δ under half the limit. The cause is the number of values: Welch's test on 3 seeds against 4 reference means has 3 to 5 degrees of freedom. The spread between references is not the cause, because the SD between reference means is close to the seed SD / √3.
4. The run-on rule spends d1024 runs that cannot produce a final yes. It sent 26 of the 78 sources judged at d1024, all no at d512 and d768. 3 of the 26 read yes at d1024, and each ends `mixed`, because a final yes also needs a yes at d768. The 26 sources cost 78 training runs (3 seeds each) of about 45 min on 8 H100s.

### Data checks

- hplt_v3 and Nemotron CC v2.1 `*_translated` are English text (100% ASCII in sampled rows). Their `helps` fits the English web category.
- Format learning: eval-format markers ("the answer is", multiple-choice options) in 600 sampled rows per source correlate with math gains (Spearman −0.45 with GSM8K), but they track math content. Sources in eval format without math content gain little (nemotron_specialized_v1_1-multiple_choice moves no task by more than 3%). We found no evidence that format alone drives a verdict.
- Contamination: the decontamination flag rate correlates with gain Δ (Spearman −0.27 to −0.57), but it is confounded with domain. A real scan is #11480.
- The base mix is Datakit text. We have not checked whether it already contains each candidate.

### Proposed judge changes

1. Drop CruxEval-O from the code group, or down-weight it.
2. Train 4 more dilution references, to give the harm test 8 reference values (#11481).
3. Narrow the run-on rule so that it only sends sources whose d768 verdict could still pair with a yes, or remove it.
4. Use more than 3 control seeds at d1024, or pool the control's seed variance across rungs, so one rung's 3-seed spread does not decide calls near the floor.

## Links

* PR: #11019 (merged into main, judge at `cc81637340`)
* W&B: runs `dbelay-main-<rung>-<source>-s<seed>` in [marin-community/marin_moe](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe); vanilla runs are `dbelay-<rung>-...`
* Choice scores: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/data_belay/choice/` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Fmarin%2Fdata_belay%2Fchoice%2F))
* Follow-ups: #11478, #11479, #11480, #11481

## Decision Log

- 2026-11-14: tests T1 to T7 fixed before the first run.
- 2026-11-14: harm limits computed from the d512 controls (max of 1% and 2.5 control seed SDs). `report` refuses a share that has no references.
- 2026-11-14: CC BY, CC BY-SA and ODC-By licenses allowed.

## Conclusion

The judge separates sources by content, repeats across seeds, rungs and model families, and reads `no gain` on null and reference arms. Calls near the 1% floor are not stable at 3 seeds, especially at d1024 and in the knowledge group. d1024 results are in the comment linked in the TL;DR.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
Concurrent cold-cache calls to `marin.datakit.decon._load_bloom` share `<cache-key>.<pid>.partial`. Local Zephyr workers run as threads in one process, so they can truncate the same temporary file and race its rename. A regional scan observed four shard retries: two `ValueError: Invalid bloom filter data` failures and two `FileNotFoundError` failures in `os.replace(partial_path, local_path)`.

Reproduce:
1. Create a valid `dupekit.Bloom` file and use an empty local Bloom cache.
2. Call `_load_bloom` for that file from four threads in one process. Synchronize the underlying source reads so all callers enter the cold-cache fill before any completes.
3. Release the reads. The shared temporary path is renamed by one caller; other callers can read a truncated file or fail to rename it.

Expected: every caller loads the complete original filter. Concurrent cache fills must use independent temporary paths and publish complete files atomically, preserving the filter bytes and membership results.

The affected implementation is present on main at `lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/decon.py:224–239`. The observed Iris job is named `new-rl-ingest-b-polaris-full-shared-lexical-v1` in cw-us-east-02a; failures occurred at 2026-11-16 21:01:29–31 UTC. [Redacted traces and the regional byte proof](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Fmarin%2Frl-data%2Fatlas%2Fingest-b%2Fpolaris%2F2026.11.16.1%2Fissue-evidence%2Fbloom-cache-race-redacted-evidence-v1.txt) are retained at `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/rl-data/atlas/ingest-b/polaris/2026.11.16.1/issue-evidence/bloom-cache-race-redacted-evidence-v1.txt`. The observed scan continues after automatic retries; a read-only check inside its regional task found the final cache and frozen S3 object identical: 269,579,775 bytes, SHA-256 `70fbe0bfd4b7ab6018461799605cb0609ae22e9043882f1fad7cf51d5730d817`. No incorrect scan result is established by this report.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

`_load_bloom` uses an LRU cache, but concurrent misses can still execute the function in separate threads. All threads in one process write the same `<cache-key>.<pid>.partial` file, so one rename can remove another caller's source while writes can overlap. No open PR addresses this cache race.

**Relevant code**
- [`decon.py#L224-L239`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/decon.py#L224-L239) — cache fill and atomic publication.

# Proposed Fix

Give each cold-cache call its own temporary path inside the cache directory, then atomically rename the complete file to the shared cache path. Add a synchronized four-thread regression that checks successful loads, membership, and cached bytes.

comments.body: 🤖 Fix is in #11565. A synchronized four-thread regression reproduced the `FileNotFoundError` before the change and passes with source-identical cached bytes; 112 affected safe tests passed, with 5 expected failures. The mandatory advisory lint review found no issues.

issues.title: [nightly-gsm8k-h100-and-grug-megatron-h100] scheduled run failing

issues.author: muchanem
issues.body:
On cw-us-east-02a, sandbox jobs are scheduled onto `gd-8xh100ib-i128` GPU nodes, which carry `node.coreweave.cloud/gvisor=true`, and never start. These are `CONTAINER_PROFILE_SANDBOX` jobs, not the legacy `GVISOR` profile #9855 keeps temporarily; the Kubernetes backend gives both profiles `runtimeClassName: gvisor`. The kubelet retries pod sandbox creation every 10-15 s with:

```
Failed to create pod sandbox: rpc error: code = Unknown desc = failed to start sandbox "<id>": failed to create containerd task: failed to create shim task: OCI runtime create failed: creating container: cannot create sandbox: cannot read client sync file: waiting for sandbox to start: EOF
```

The pod stays in `ContainerCreating` until the caller gives up. On 2026-10-13, a Taskforge queue job on 02a lost all 4 of its build machines: each sat in `ContainerCreating` until shellbox's 600 s scheduling timeout. I read node and events for one of them, which is where the error above comes from; the earlier pods' events had already expired. The machine image was the public `docker.io/library/python@sha256:a6e34c598f2467ed0e9a8d349809fcd8b5c603269512df273a0bb1784edc11b1` (python:3.12-slim). The same sandbox spec and image start on cw-rno2a, where gVisor sandboxes were measured at 512 concurrent with no failures, so the run moved there.

Of the 36 nodes labelled gVisor-capable on 02a, 32 are H100 nodes. Only 4 are CPU nodes: 3 in Iris pool `cpu-genoa`, plus 1 with no pool label. Sandbox jobs request CPU and memory only, so nothing keeps them off the GPU nodes. #9696 covers an earlier 02a failure in which leaked `runsc` sandboxes exhausted node cgroups; that may be related, but I have not checked cgroup counts on the affected node.

Expected: a sandbox job on 02a starts on a node where `runsc` works.

Done when either the H100 nodes no longer advertise gVisor or `runsc` starts sandboxes on them, and 02a has enough CPU gVisor capacity for sandbox workloads (a Taskforge queue runs up to a few hundred concurrent sandboxes).

The same error has recurred on 02a since 2026-10-06 ([incident 631](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/631)). Every failing node recorded there (g83d142, g73b892, g856b8a, g82d828) and this one (g8247ba) is a `gd-8xh100ib-i128` node.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

Iris maps both `CONTAINER_PROFILE_SANDBOX` and legacy `GVISOR` to RuntimeClass `gvisor`, with no profile-specific node selector; the CoreWeave-managed RuntimeClass selects any node labeled `node.coreweave.cloud/gvisor=true`. That permits the reported H100 placement but does not explain the `runsc` startup EOF. [Incident 631](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/631) reproduced the EOF with public and base images on 02a while the same probes started on cw-rno2a, so an image pull or longer scheduling wait is unlikely to fix it. The live NodePools report 4 CPU and 32 H100 nodes; this session cannot read individual nodes or the ClusterQueue because its Kubernetes role forbids those requests.

**Relevant code**
- [`tasks.py#L1068-L1078`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/9a030a9df36cf7d095650ed7561d68812ea0ef4a/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L1068-L1078) — RuntimeClass and node selector.
- [`kueue_manifests.py#L96-L100`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/9a030a9df36cf7d095650ed7561d68812ea0ef4a/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/k8s/kueue_manifests.py#L96-L100) — one flavor spans CPU and GPU pools.
- [`cw-us-east-02a.yaml#L176-L217`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/9a030a9df36cf7d095650ed7561d68812ea0ef4a/lib/iris/config/cw-us-east-02a.yaml#L176-L217) — four CPU and 32 H100 nodes.

# Proposed Fix

1. With node-read access, compare a failing H100 node with a CPU node, including a bounded `gvisor` startup probe on the CPU node. Record their gVisor labels, taints, `runsc` and containerd versions/configuration, kubelet and runtime errors, and cgroup counts. Check whether the cgroup exhaustion from [#9696](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9696) recurred; the current EOF alone does not establish that cause.
2. Repair the H100 `runsc` setup and prove a sandbox starts there, or remove the gVisor label at its CoreWeave-owned source so RuntimeClass cannot select those nodes. Check the fourth CPU node's label and runtime before making it eligible. Keep any Iris placement change in a separate PR only if node labels cannot express the verified runtime capability.
3. Compare the allocatable CPU and memory on healthy gVisor nodes, Kueue quota, and existing load with the actual Taskforge per-pod requests at its peak concurrency of a few hundred. Increase healthy CPU capacity or fix H100 runtime if the four CPU nodes cannot admit that load.
4. Run one public-image sandbox canary, then a bounded Taskforge-scale batch on 02a. Require all admitted pods to reach Running within the 600 s scheduling budget, no `FailedCreatePodSandBox` EOF events, and stable shim/cgroup counts after teardown. Record the node and quota measurements in this issue before declaring the incident fixed.

issues.title: [iris] gVisor sandbox pods fail to start on cw-us-east-02a H100 nodes

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
On cw-us-east-02a, `CONTAINER_PROFILE_SANDBOX` pods placed on the `cpu-genoa` pool (`cd-gp-a192-genoa`) never start. The kubelet reports:

```
/usr/local/bin/nvidia-container-runtime-gvisor did not terminate successfully
```

The runtime's `log.json` could not be retrieved, so the underlying cause is unknown. These are CPU-only nodes, but the gVisor RuntimeClass handler on them runs through NVIDIA's gVisor wrapper.

#10090 covers the different startup failure on the same cluster's H100 nodes (`cannot read client sync file: waiting for sandbox to start: EOF`). It expects the CPU nodes to carry sandbox workloads once the H100 nodes stop taking them. With this failure, 02a has no node where a SANDBOX pod starts. This blocks per-task Kubernetes storage enforcement for Harbor tasks (#11336, #11342), because shellbox's Iris backend submits every machine as SANDBOX.

Reproduce:
1. Submit a CPU-only Iris job with `container_profile=CONTAINER_PROFILE_SANDBOX` to cw-us-east-02a, constrained to the `cpu-genoa` pool. `/benfeuer/atlas-storage-overflow-20261113-v5` is a killed example.
2. The task stays in `ContainerCreating`. The pod events show the error above.

Expected: a SANDBOX pod on a `cpu-genoa` node starts under `runsc`, as the same spec does on cw-rno2a.

The same day, a non-SANDBOX CPU pod on 02a started normally and was evicted at its 1 GiB ephemeral-storage limit, so the storage limit itself works there. Evidence and job IDs: [incident 976](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/976).

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
A CoreWeave Iris job that uses a non-SANDBOX container profile and `EGRESS_POLICY_NONE` fails in the `stage-workdir` init container. The init container fetches the workspace bundle from the controller, and egress NONE blocks that connection. The task never starts.

The client always sends a workspace bundle for a non-SANDBOX profile (`lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/client/remote_client.py:210`). If every file is excluded, the bundle is still a valid zip with no entries, so the controller stores it and the pod still gets the init container. Only SANDBOX skips the bundle. Thus there is no way to submit a non-SANDBOX egress-NONE job.

This matters now because SANDBOX pods do not start on cw-us-east-02a (#11343). For an untrusted-code job on 02a, the fallback is RESTRICTED with egress NONE, and that combination fails as shown here.

Reproduce:
1. On cw-us-east-02a, submit a CPU job with `container_profile=CONTAINER_PROFILE_RESTRICTED` and `egress_policy=EGRESS_POLICY_NONE`. Use an image that already holds the code, and exclude all workspace files.
2. The attempt fails with `Init:Error stage-workdir` and an HTTP error from `http.client` (`self.endheaders(...)`). `/benfeuer/sft-audit-repro-exec-20261117-063043` is an example.

Expected: a job that does not need a workspace can run with egress NONE. The pod gets no `stage-workdir` init container.

A local client-side change makes the job run: if the workspace zip has no entries, the client sends an empty `bundle_blob`. Then the controller stores no bundle and `_build_init_container_spec` adds no init container. Other possible fixes:
- An explicit "no workspace" option on submit.
- Rejection at submit time when a non-SANDBOX egress-NONE job carries a bundle, with a clear error, so the failure does not show as `Init:Error`.

comments.body:

# Research

`create_workspace_zip()` writes a valid ZIP even when file collection returns no entries. The remote client sends those bytes, the controller stores them as a bundle, and Kubernetes adds `stage-workdir`; egress NONE then blocks its controller fetch. No open PR overlaps this failure.

**Relevant code**
- [`bundle.py#L101-L128`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/client/bundle.py#L101-L128) — creates the empty ZIP.
- [`remote_client.py#L198-L204`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/client/remote_client.py#L198-L204) — sends bundle bytes.
- [`service.py#L1714-L1727`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/service.py#L1714-L1727) — stores nonempty bundles.
- [`tasks.py#L532-L538`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L532-L538) — adds staging when a bundle exists.

# Proposed Fix

Return empty bytes from `create_workspace_zip()` when file collection is empty. The existing client and controller paths will then omit the bundle, leaving no `stage-workdir` init container for a workspace-free job. Add a regression test for empty and nonempty workspaces.

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
After Harbor applies the agent network policy to a running Daytona sandbox, a new TCP connection to the probe host sometimes still succeeds. In a 1600-trial TMax pilot (Qwen3.6-27B, terminus-2, Daytona EVAL org, 64 concurrent trials), 9 trials (0.56%) failed with `NetworkLockdownError: pypi.org:443 is still reachable after the agent network policy`. All 9 failed closed: the trial stopped before the agent started, so no agent ran with open egress. Each failed trial is lost and has to be run again.

The policy is a domain allow-list containing only `iris.oa.dev`. Harbor calls `DaytonaMachine.update_network` ([machine.py:298](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f07e07ac26ef2457f98cb7a7adfa7e96e9c031a0/lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/backends/daytona/machine.py#L298)), which awaits `sandbox.update_network_settings`. It then probes `timeout 10 bash -c 'exec 3<>/dev/tcp/pypi.org/443'` ([daytona.py:285-300](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f07e07ac26ef2457f98cb7a7adfa7e96e9c031a0/vendor/harbor/src/harbor/environments/daytona.py#L285-L300)). A probe exit code of 0 raises the error. Both code paths are on the pilot branch `task/qwen36-tmax-pilot`, not on main.

Reproduce:
1. Start a Daytona sandbox with an unrestricted network policy.
2. Call `update_network` with `DaytonaNetworkPolicy(DOMAIN_ALLOW_LIST, "iris.oa.dev")`.
3. Immediately open a TCP connection to `pypi.org:443`. About 1 in 180 sandboxes accepts it.

Expected: once `update_network_settings` returns, the policy is in force, or the API gives a way to wait until it is.

Failed trials (finish times 2026-11-14 UTC):

| Trial | Finished |
|---|---|
| task_007905_85674759__Z6SBrB3 | 03:48:57 |
| task_005909_4d8203db__rEaeamb | 04:00:05 |
| task_006798_b7fc9154__QGjb56f | 04:01:15 |
| task_009570_fa1c4ca2__UVKHmWS | 04:04:07 |
| task_004838_4a013d26__iQLiwBu | 04:13:53 |
| task_009458_1bff453d__i7BQkai | 04:32:49 |
| task_009761_7f37c29a__JuEwwPr | 05:02:06 |
| task_005979_2298ae0c__FfAiEVf | 05:12:22 |
| task_006347_d2193fb9__ueDxzAA | 05:12:55 |

Observations:
- **The failures are spread over the run, not clustered.**
- **They don't repeat on the same task.** No task failed this way twice. Task 006798's second attempt hit a different error, an apply failure.
- **The cause is unknown.** It may be a propagation delay after `update_network_settings` returns (inferred, not confirmed).
- **One-sandbox smoke checks passed every time.** In them, a held connection and new connections were all blocked after the update (`experiments/post_training/tmax_reserve/lockdown_smoke.py` on the same branch).
- **The rest of the run's lockdowns held.** 4 other trials failed to apply the policy at all, each with `DaytonaConnectionError: Failed to update network settings: [Errno 104] Connection reset by peer`. That is a transient API failure that retries would cover.
- **No apt traffic reached the mirror** in any of the 1600 trials.

Results root: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/qwen36-tmax-pilot/pilot-8h-v1/` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Fqwen36-tmax-pilot%2Fpilot-8h-v1%2F)). Each trial's `result.json` holds the full traceback.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

On `task/qwen36-tmax-pilot`, Harbor waits for Daytona's network update and treats one successful `/dev/tcp/pypi.org/443` connect as a lockdown failure; the nine errors establish only that this TCP connect returned zero. [Daytona's network documentation](https://www.daytona.io/docs/en/network-limits/#https-traffic) says its domain allow list enforces HTTPS by host name through an egress proxy, so the TCP result alone does not establish that an HTTPS request reached PyPI. The smoke test waits 20 seconds after the update before probing; it cannot distinguish TCP-only success from update propagation delay. I found no overlapping open PR.

**Relevant code**
- [machine.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f07e07ac26ef2457f98cb7a7adfa7e96e9c031a0/lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/backends/daytona/machine.py#L298-L300) — awaits the SDK update
- [daytona.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f07e07ac26ef2457f98cb7a7adfa7e96e9c031a0/vendor/harbor/src/harbor/environments/daytona.py#L277-L305) — single TCP probe and startup gate
- [trial.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f07e07ac26ef2457f98cb7a7adfa7e96e9c031a0/vendor/harbor/src/harbor/trial/trial.py#L1356-L1365) — lockdown before agent launch
- [lockdown_smoke.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f07e07ac26ef2457f98cb7a7adfa7e96e9c031a0/experiments/post_training/tmax_reserve/lockdown_smoke.py#L98-L121) — delayed probe

# Proposed Fix

1. Reproduce at the pilot's 64-concurrent-sandbox setting. Record the update-return time, immediate and repeated TCP results, a request for recognizable PyPI content, an allow-listed `iris.oa.dev` control request, and sandbox IDs. Keep agents stopped during diagnostics; classify proxy denial, upstream content, and inconclusive requests separately.
2. If TCP succeeds while the proxy denies HTTPS, replace the TCP-only gate with a probe that recognizes the denial and fails closed on inconclusive results. Add a behavioral regression test.
3. If PyPI content is reachable after the update, measure how long it remains reachable, report sandbox IDs and timestamps to Daytona, and add a bounded verification wait that never starts the agent while the probe is reachable or inconclusive.
4. Validate on a comparable 64-concurrent cohort with enough updates to compare against the pilot's 9/1600 failures. Report the observed failure rate and any confirmed disallowed HTTPS responses.

comments.body:
🤖 Independent confirmation from the Atlas backend-survey live qualification (2026-11-17), via a different code path: `shellbox`'s `DaytonaMachineFactory` creates the sandbox with `network_block_all=True` in the create parameters (`_sandbox_parameters`, both the factory-policy and spec-driven paths — verified the parameter reaches `client.create`), and a raw TCP connect from inside the sandbox still succeeded.

Reproduce:
1. Create a Daytona sandbox with `network_block_all: true` in the create parameters.
2. From inside the sandbox: `socket.create_connection(('1.1.1.1', 443), timeout=10)` — succeeds.
3. `socket.getaddrinfo('example.com', 443)` — fails (gaierror): DNS resolution is blocked, direct-IP TCP egress is not.

Observed: `tcp:connected; dns:gaierror` — the block intercepts DNS resolution but direct-IP TCP egress bypasses it.

Expected: `network_block_all` blocks raw TCP egress as well as DNS.

Typed evidence: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/rl-data/atlas/backend-surveys/20261117-live-qualification/daytona-evidence.json` (probe `egress_deny`, outcome `leaked`, sandbox created and deleted by the same process). comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
🤖 **CORRECTION to my earlier comment (2026-11-17 10:14Z)** — the coordinator's hypothesis was right, and a rigorous 5-round repro with a control sandbox reverses my "leak" call.

Method (clean script, Daytona SDK 0.200.2 only, no shellbox/harbor code): per round, two sandboxes from the same pinned image — one with `network_block_all=true`, one default as control. Five probes from inside each: raw TCP connect to 1.1.1.1:443, TLS handshake capturing the peer certificate subject, HTTP GET to 1.1.1.1 with status + body bytes, a raw UDP DNS query to 1.1.1.1:53, and `getaddrinfo('example.com')`. Ten sandboxes total, each deleted by exact ID; per-run results: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/rl-data/atlas/backend-surveys/20261117-live-qualification/daytona-egress-repro-5runs.jsonl`.

Results (5/5 rounds identical): under `network_block_all` the TCP connect **succeeds** (peer 1.1.1.1:443) — but that is a transparent egress proxy accepting the connection, not a path. The TLS handshake dies with `SSLEOFError` (no real certificate — the control sandbox gets the genuine Cloudflare subject every round), the HTTP response is empty (the control gets `HTTP/1.1 301` + body), `getaddrinfo` fails (`gaierror`), and the raw UDP query's 29-byte answer is a synthesized stub (the control's real answer is 61 bytes). **No bytes from the real 1.1.1.1 ever came back under block_all.**

Verdict: `network_block_all` effectively blocks egress — the connect-only artifact is the proxy interception the loom research described, not a leak. My earlier comment mistook the proxy's TCP accept for a bypass; the capability survey grades Daytona network-deny SUPPORTED on this evidence.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body: 🤖 Closing: not a Daytona leak. Under `network_block_all`, a transparent egress proxy accepts the TCP connect but forwards no data: TLS is dropped with no certificate, HTTP returns empty, and DNS is blocked. A control sandbox gets real responses in each probe. The clean 5-round repro and its results are in the correction comment above. A lockdown check must send data; a TCP connect alone does not show egress. The connect-only probe is only on `task/qwen36-tmax-pilot`, not on main.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
Several agents can run as the same Iris user. Iris authorizes owner-gated actions per user, so any agent, or any task that one of the user's jobs runs, can cancel, complete, kick or exec into all jobs of that user. One agent can therefore kill another agent's jobs by mistake.

Today the only protection is a local client-side wrapper that refuses cancellations outside an agent's job prefix. That wrapper protects only agents that use it. An agent that calls `iris job cancel` directly is not blocked, because its token carries the full user identity.

Proposed design (draft PR #11588; not scheduled now):
- A bearer token scoped to a job-name prefix (for example `/benfeuer/exp2-`). It authenticates as the user, but owner-gated actions reach only jobs under the prefix.
- The controller stores the prefix on the job at admission and gives it to the job's task tokens, so a scoped job cannot act outside its subtree.
- A scoped token cannot mint a token that is wider than itself, and it never carries admin authority. A malformed prefix claim denies the token.
- The TTL is bounded, because scoped tokens cannot be revoked.

This is a large change: it needs a controller migration and a rollout. Defer it until there is bandwidth.

Done when:
- A token scoped to one prefix cannot cancel, complete, kick or exec into a job outside that prefix. A test shows this.
- A task of a scoped job gets the same restriction.
- Unscoped and admin tokens behave as before.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

Iris currently checks the job owner by user ID, so two agents sharing one Iris user can authorize actions on each other's jobs. [Draft PR #11588](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11588) already implements prefix claims, controller gates, task-token inheritance, federation propagation, and a job-row migration; it remains a draft. Its [review](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11588#issuecomment-6950133465) identified remaining scope questions around task-token minting and proxy routes.

**Relevant code**
- [`authorize_resource_owner`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/rpc/auth.py#L151-L160) — user-level owner check.
- [`_authorize_job_owner`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/service.py#L1221-L1228) — controller job gate.
- [`authorize_mapping`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/rust/src/lib.rs#L930-L952) — proxy route gate.

# Proposed Fix

Continue #11588 when this work is scheduled; avoid a second implementation PR.

1. Finish the prefix boundary at every owner-gated action, including `/proxy` routes resolved to another job's task. A scoped bearer should receive a denial before reaching an out-of-prefix actor or service endpoint.
2. Keep scoped-token delegation narrowing to sub-prefixes. Deny `MintScopedToken` from task identities so a task token cannot become a longer-lived user credential. Preserve the existing unscoped-user and admin behavior.
3. Verify the prefix survives admission, persisted job rows, retries, task-token minting, and federated handoff. Add regression tests for out-of-prefix cancel, complete, kick, exec, endpoint mint and proxy access, plus malformed claims, scope widening, and a task attempting to mint.
4. Run Iris Python and Rust tests, migration tests, lint review, and PR CI. Before any rollout, test two agents under one user on a non-production controller, including a pre-migration job. Keep controller deployment separate from this issue's deferred implementation decision.

Open decision for the PR: whether any task needs scoped-token minting. If so, its minted token must expire no later than the caller's credential.

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
🤖 An agent literature survey for the Mochi post-training recipe found two Nemotron-sourced changes for train/inference mismatch in async MoE RL. Mochi RL already uses one of them (router replay). The other, an FP32 LM head, has not been tested by us. Nothing here was measured empirically on Mochi: this is a pointer for the RL team, not a result.

**What Nemotron reports**
- The [Nemotron 3.5 Super/Lightning technical report](https://research.nvidia.com/labs/nemotron/files/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Super-and-Lightning-Technical-Report.pdf) (RL section) says router replay plus an FP32 LM head "reduce the KL error between the training and inference engines by more than an order of magnitude". The two are reported together, so the report does not say how much each one contributes.
- Aside: the [HF MoE handbook](https://huggingface-moe-blogpost.hf.space/) says the NeMo-RL recipes for Nemotron 3 Super/Ultra freeze the router matrix in async RL and keep the load-balancing bias live, and that "whether replay pays off in reward is still contested". Router freezing is an alternative or a complement to replay.

**Where Mochi stands (from existing work, not new measurements)**
- Router replay: Mochi (Hero) RL already uses captured-route replay, and it passed the recorded 4K RL gate in https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10388. Its measured replay result is batch-order sensitivity of the gradient: 71.96% → 1.37% at PP48, with +5.3% scoring-plus-update time. That is not a serve-vs-trainer logprob gap, and the same issue notes that serving–trainer differences persist.
- Bit-identical numerics: the stack beginning with https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10634 was closed in favour of score centering with TIS (https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11066, open), with probes in https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10658 (open). The Mochi RL launcher is https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11321 (draft).
- FP32 LM head, serving side: the pinned vLLM fork (`0ac9dcb`) already supports it. `vllm/model_executor/layers/logits_processor.py` reads `--hf-overrides '{"head_dtype": "float32"}'` and accumulates the head GEMM into FP32. Its comment says this is "required for RL training-inference consistency". The Mochi serve config (`experiments/evaluation/mochi/model-mochi-sft-step400407.yaml`) does not set it, so served logits are BF16.
- FP32 LM head, trainer side: SkyRL's Megatron wrapper calls the model with `fp32_output=False` (`vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/workers/megatron/megatron_model_wrapper.py`), so trainer logits are BF16 too. Matching vLLM would need a Megatron-side FP32 output projection, which is not checked here.
- Related Snowball evidence, not RL and not Mochi: in an Oct 25 Levanter-vs-vLLM scoring check on Snowball, silent MoE token drops and BF16 combine weights were each separate numerics boundaries. Fixing them one at a time cut the p99 per-token logprob gap from 3.96 to 0.60 nats.

**What we did not do:** no empirical study on Mochi of the FP32 head, router freezing, or replay versus no replay. The survey proposed a 1 h arm; it moves off our list and into this issue.

Done when: the RL team decides whether to test an FP32 LM head on both engines (vLLM `head_dtype` plus a Megatron FP32 output projection) on Mochi, measured as the serve-vs-trainer logprob or KL gap on fixed responses with replay on, and records the decision here. Router freezing is optional, as a separate arm.

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
## Read this before running SFT on TPU

- **Measured throughput** at 8k context: 266 positions/s per chip on v4-128 (64 chips), 242 on v4-256 (128 chips). TPU is not faster than H100.
- **An E12-size arm** (15 updates × 8.39M positions) takes ≈2 h of compute on v4-128 at that rate (arithmetic), against 11–31 min measured on 64 H100.
- **A 150-update arm** is ≈11–12 h on v4-256 (estimate from the 8k rate). Slices below v4-256 are not practical for real arms.
- **Use TPU as an overflow venue** when H100s are blocked, not for speed.
- **Both attention fixes are required:** PR 11506 (packed rows with context parallelism fail to compile without it) and PR 11507 (without it, local-window layers silently train as full attention, so the run trains a different model).
- **Not yet qualified on TPU:** 262,144-token rows (the recipe's length; only 8k has run), checkpoint restore, and any quality match against H100. A matched TPU-vs-H100 run is in progress.

## Summary

Snowball (67B MoE) long-loop SFT now trains on TPU v4. A 20-update run on a v4-128 slice (64 chips) finished on 2026-11-15 with finite losses and a written checkpoint. This issue records what works, what was fixed, and what is still unproven, so others can use the TPU cluster for SFT.

## Result

Setup: long-loop SFT recipe, 16 hosts x 4 chips (v4-128), small test batch of 131,072 token positions per update. Init: the Snowball **pretraining** base (long-context checkpoint at step 157,000), not the 10/05 SFT model. This is checked in the code for the 1-update window-fix run, the 20-update v4-128 run and the later 20-update v4-256 run. The fit-proxy row's code was not re-checked.

| Run | Updates | Outcome |
|---|---:|---|
| Fit proxy (all layers global attention) | 1 | Succeeded, 8.99 chip-hours |
| Real recipe with window fix | 1 | Succeeded, 9.14 chip-hours |
| Real recipe with window fix | 20 | Succeeded, 15.04 chip-hours |

Measured on the 20-update run:

- 7.70 s per update in steady state, 17,029 token positions per second (266 per chip).
- End to end 847 s, including compile (about 33-36 s) and checkpoint write.
- Checkpoint: 801 GB in 584 objects; write and drain took 191 s.
- 20 finite loss rows; all 16 hosts succeeded.

## Fixes needed to get there

- **Segment IDs were sharded differently from the query inputs** under context parallelism, which failed at trace time (`Invalid shape for q segment_ids: (8192,). Expected: (2048,)`). Fix: PR 11506 (draft).
- **TPU Splash attention ignored the per-layer local window**, so local layers ran full causal attention. A 2-layer CPU probe showed a max logit difference of 6.4e-3 against the reference, and 1.5e-7 after the fix. Tracked in issue 11502; fix for the long-loop branch in PR 11507 (draft). The same pattern exists in other model files on main.
- **`mixture_block_size` must divide the stage start index.** The data config value is sized for batch 256; a small batch needs a smaller block.

## Limits

- **Not a matched speed comparison.** Three unrelated 64-H100 SFT arms measured 1,044-2,907 positions per second per H100, against 266 per v4 chip here. The TPU run used a small untuned batch, and nothing was measured per dollar.
- **Only v4-128 was tried.** Scaling to v4-512 or larger is not measured.
- **No TPU-trained checkpoint has been evaluated.** Equal quality to an H100-trained checkpoint is not shown.
- The per-host sharding dump and actual dtypes were not captured in the first runs.

## Next steps

- [ ] One run of at most 1 hour on the largest available v4 slice with the full recipe batch; report positions per second in total and per chip.
- [ ] One matched SFT arm on TPU and on H100, scored on the same evals.
- [ ] Land the two fix pull requests and close the remaining model-file issue:
  - #11506 (segment IDs under context parallelism, against main)
  - #11507 (per-layer local windows in TPU Splash attention, against the long-loop branch)
  - #11502 (same window bug in the Grug models on main, still open)
- [ ] If both hold, document the TPU SFT launch path next to the long-loop recipe.

## Corrections

- 2026-11-17: init was misstated as the 10/05 checkpoint. The TPU runs started from the Snowball pretraining base (step 157,000).

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 Two TPU attention bugs in the SFT path, in plain English. Both block SFT on TPU. The fixes are open as draft PRs.

```
local layer:   each token sees only the last 2,048 tokens   [.....####]
global layer:  each token sees everything before it         [#########]
the model alternates them across depth; both stay inside one packed document
```

## PR 11507: local layers silently ran as global layers
- **What the model does:** some layers look only at a recent window of tokens (local) and others look at everything before (global). The runtime picks the window per layer inside a scanned loop.
- **What went wrong on TPU:** the TPU attention kernel (Splash) reads only a fixed mask. It ignored the per-layer window, so every local layer ran full causal attention.
- **How you would notice:** you would not. Nothing fails; training runs and the loss looks normal.
- **Does it block SFT?** Yes. A TPU run silently trains a different model: full causal attention in the local layers.
- **The fix:** build two fixed masks, local and global, and pick one per layer from the existing global flag. Document boundaries in packed rows are still kept.
- **Still unfixed:** Grug models on main use the same pattern (issue 11502 stays open). This PR covers only the long-loop SFT runtime.
- **Test evidence:** a two-layer CPU Splash-interpreter regression matches an independent reference to under 1e-6 (max abs logit difference). It fails if local attention is replaced by full causal. In issue 11502's probe the unfixed path differed by 6.36e-3, and the fixed masks by 1.49e-7.

## PR 11506: document IDs mis-sharded under context parallelism
- **What the model does:** many documents are packed into one long row. Segment IDs stop a token attending across a document boundary. With context parallelism, each chip holds a slice of the row.
- **What went wrong on TPU:** queries were split across chips, but their segment IDs were not. At context parallelism 4 each chip got 2,048 queries and 8,192 segment IDs.
- **How you would notice:** it fails at trace time, before any step runs.
- **Does it block SFT?** Yes: packed rows with context parallelism above 1 cannot run on TPU.
- **The fix:** split the query segment IDs the same way as the queries, and align the key segment IDs with the gathered keys.
- **Test evidence:** CPU-interpreter tests compare packed outputs at context parallelism 4 against context parallelism 1, for causal and sliding-window masks. A negative control removes document masking and must differ. The attention module passes 15 tests, with 1 TPU-only test skipped.

**What has run on TPU:** the code that ran on TPU has the same attention and model files as the PR branches (identical file contents). That code ran in a 1-update smoke and in two 20-update runs (64 and 128 chips, context parallelism 4) without error. The TPU runs also carried changes that are not in these PRs (the TPU launcher and a weights-first model init), and the PR test files differ slightly. The evidence that the outputs are numerically correct is CPU-interpreter only. No TPU-trained model has been compared with its H100 twin yet; that is in progress.

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
Queries on the Finelog `log` table that filter on `epoch_ms` open every file. The catalog does not record each segment's time range, so the time filter cannot skip any file. Most of the query time goes to reading Parquet footers, not data. That is why day-sized scans exceed the 10-second query deadline. #11087 raises that deadline to 30 seconds as a stopgap. Once time-filtered queries can skip files, the deadline can go back down.

## Evidence

A one-hour `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on the `marin` hub (2026-11-08 23:38 UTC). It filtered `epoch_ms` to one hour, plus `LIKE` filters on `key` and `data`. Wall time was 7.1 s. Full query, plan and metrics: https://gist.github.com/karansag/160e31066556f7b00199c6b328d925f5

Table: `log` in namespace `marin`, 10.4 B rows, 324 GB, 1,977 segments. Trigram indexes on `key` and `data`. No sort columns and no partitioning.

| metric | value |
|---|---|
| files pruned by statistics | 1.66 K total, 1.66 K matched: **0 files skipped** |
| row groups pruned by footer stats | 2.49 K total, 6 matched |
| bytes scanned | 5.00 MB |
| `metadata_load_time` | 18.23 s |
| `time_elapsed_opening` | 52.41 s |
| output rows | 9 |

The times are summed across 16 parallel file groups, so they exceed the wall time.

The catalog records each segment's `seq` and `key` ranges, but not `epoch_ms`. So every file's footer is read just to get the `epoch_ms` min and max. After that, the query reads almost nothing: 6 row groups and 5 MB.

Impact: a 60-day pull of `levanter.model_cache` lines in 12-hour windows lost 58% of its windows to `snapshot read deadline exceeded`, even with three retries per window (#9233).

## Possible directions

- Record per-segment `epoch_ms` min and max in the catalog, so time filters drop files before they are opened.
- Sort or cluster segments by time during compaction, so those ranges are narrow.

## Done when

- A one-hour `epoch_ms` query on `log` opens only the segments that overlap that hour.
- The default query deadline can go back to 10 seconds, reverting #11087's increase.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

`Store::query_providers` snapshots paths only, and `NamespaceProvider` gives every path to DataFusion before the existing row-group and index pruning runs. Neither the in-memory segment record nor the SQLite catalog carries `epoch_ms` bounds. This matches the issue's one-hour plan: 1,660 files matched file statistics, then only six row groups were read.

**Relevant code**
- [`store.rs#L515-L527`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/finelog/rust/src/store/store.rs#L515-L527) — snapshots paths for query providers
- [`provider.rs#L112-L182`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/finelog/rust/src/query/provider.rs#L112-L182) — registers all paths before scan
- [`catalog.rs#L193-L207`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/finelog/rust/src/store/catalog.rs#L193-L207) — persisted segment columns
- [`namespace.rs#L735-L759`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/finelog/rust/src/store/namespace.rs#L735-L759) — flush publishes segment metadata
- [`executor.rs#L318-L334`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/finelog/rust/src/store/compaction/executor.rs#L318-L334) — compaction creates replacement metadata

# Proposed Fix

1. Measure the min/max `epoch_ms` span of current `log` segments and the overlap count for representative one-hour and one-day windows. The existing L1+ sort is by `(key, seq)`, so wide time spans could leave most files overlapping even after catalog pruning.
2. Add nullable `min_epoch_ms` and `max_epoch_ms` to the segment catalog and in-memory segment metadata. Migrate existing SQLite catalogs; derive bounds for new L0 segments from the sealed batch, carry correct bounds through compaction and level bumps, and backfill old/adopted segments from Parquet footers. A bound is usable only when every row group has complete statistics. Missing or incomplete bounds keep the segment in the scan.
3. Include bounds in the same snapshot as segment paths. For safe conjunctive `epoch_ms` comparisons, intersect the time range with those bounds and pass only overlapping paths to `ListingTable`, before DataFusion footer reads and before trigram/exact pruning. Keep the SQL predicate as a residual filter; do not infer time from `seq` or file creation time.
4. Test results and planned file groups with multiple segments, out-of-order timestamps, an old catalog, missing statistics, restart/adoption, and compaction. Benchmark the same one-hour query after backfill with maintenance quiescent. Record files opened, footer load time, and wall time; lower the raised query deadline only after representative day scans fit under 10 seconds.

No open PR found for segment time pruning. #11086 and #11087 address the deadline only. If step 1 shows most segments overlap each window, time-aware segment layout needs a separate design: changing the current `(key, seq)` layout or seq-contiguous compaction can break existing pruning and segment identity assumptions.

comments.author: HRL9000
comments.body:
🤖 **Design: in-catalog min/max bounds for declared columns, like key bounds**

This matches **proposed fix 2** in the [research comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11172#issuecomment-6773719532): per-segment `epoch_ms` bounds in the catalog, filled at write, carried through compaction and level bumps, and backfilled from footers. A segment without bounds stays in the scan. Two notes on the other fixes there:

- **Fix 1 (measure segment time spans) is done: the measurements are below.** Segments are already narrow in time: across all ~1,940 live `log` files the median spans 0.5 h, p99 8.7 h and the maximum 33 h. Replaying this issue's hour against per-file bounds keeps 2 files out of ~1,660. Details are under Background below.
- **Fix 3 is more general than the snapshot detail.** The general requirement is that the query engine uses the segments' min/max statistics correctly before opening files; carrying bounds with the segment paths is one way to do that. DataFusion can already skip files from per-file statistics it is given; today Finelog gives it none from the catalog, so it has to read every footer to find them.

The design follows. It covers background, proposal, success criteria, approach, rollout, timeframe and alternatives.

### Background and Motivation

A one-hour query on `log` is slow because Finelog opens almost every file in the table to find the few that hold that hour.

- **The query.** An `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` of a one-hour `log` search opened about 1,660 files, and the `epoch_ms` filter pruned none of them. After the footers were read, only 6 row groups and 5 MB were scanned. Three hub reports for similar searches show 2,313–2,379 candidate files and 6.8–8.7 s each.
- **Why the `epoch_ms` filter pruned no file.** Before it opens files, Finelog can drop a segment by its key-column bounds, its `seq` bounds or its partition. For `log` the `epoch_ms` filter matches none of these. `log`'s key column is `key` (the log source, a string), so the catalog has no `epoch_ms` bounds, and `log` is not partitioned. The key column does two jobs, sort order and catalog bounds, and `log` chose `key` for fast per-source reads.
- **Pruning by `epoch_ms` min/max would be effective, because each file covers a short time span.** `log` has about 1,940 live files. The median file spans 0.5 h, p99 8.7 h, maximum 33 h. With per-file `epoch_ms` min/max in the catalog, the issue's hour would keep 2 files instead of about 1,660.

### Proposal

Today the catalog keeps min/max bounds for one column per table, the key column (key bounds), and query planning prunes segments by them. This proposal lets a table declare more columns that get the same in-catalog bounds. They become part of the segment list that the server keeps in memory for each table, so planning drops a segment before it opens the file, with no footer read.

- **Opt-in per column.** Bounds on every column would fit (an estimated 12–39 MB on top of about 60 MB of catalog), but most columns do not prune: each file covers nearly their full range.
- **Start with time columns.** About 65 bytes per segment: about 0.7 MB for the whole hub (about 1% of the catalog).

#### Which tables benefit

Files still opened for a window from the lookback start until now, with the share skipped:

| Table | GiB | Files | Time column | 1h | 6h | 1d | 7d | Needs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `log` | 302.7 | 1,935 | `epoch_ms` INT64 | 62 (97%) | 69 (96%) | 103 (95%) | 169 (91%) | step 1 |
| `iris.worker` | 27.5 | 233 | `ts` | 51 (78%) | 53 (77%) | 54 (77%) | 62 (73%) | steps 1, 2 |
| `zephyr.worker` | 14.2 | 185 | `ts` | 29 (84%) | 41 (78%) | 60 (68%) | 67 (64%) | steps 1, 2 |
| `iris.task` | 11.0 | 327 | `ts` | 63 (81%) | 80 (76%) | 90 (72%) | 106 (68%) | steps 1, 2 |
| `iris.profile` | 7.7 | 155 | `captured_at` | 17 (89%) | 19 (88%) | 30 (81%) | 34 (78%) | steps 1, 2 |

- **Already pruned by time:** `levanter.metrics`, `telemetry_v1.node_agent`, `telemetry_v1.marinskyrl` and `telemetry_v1.vllm` (332 GiB). Their key is `timestamp_ms`, which is `INT64`, and the Grafana queries filter it with integer literals (`timestamp_ms >= {start_ms}`). Those filters reach the key-bound check today.
- The issue's hour was in the past, so only compacted files overlap it (2). A window ending now also keeps the 30–60 recent files that are not compacted yet, which is why the 1h column shows 62 for `log`. By bytes, the skip is 97% or more through 1d.

### Success

Success is achieved when:

1. On the hub, the issue's one-hour `log` query opens fewer than 100 files instead of about 1,660–2,370.
2. `iris.task` and `iris.worker` show the same kind of drop for one-hour `ts` filters.
3. Query results never change. The first implementation has tests that check this while bounds are absent or partial: a table where no segment has bounds yet, a mix of segments with and without bounds (as during the backfill), and the same after the backfill. Each test asserts that a time-filtered query returns exactly the rows it returns with pruning turned off.

Wall time is measured but is not a gate, because the exact cause of the 7 s is still open.

### Approach

**Step 1: bounds on `log`** (success 1 and 3)

1. Add a `catalog_bounds` column flag to the table spec, and set it on `log`'s `epoch_ms`.
2. Store each flagged column's min and max per segment in the catalog. Fill them when Finelog writes a segment.
3. Add a maintenance task that reads the footers of existing segments once and fills their bounds. Most of `log` is never rewritten, so this is needed.
4. In planning, drop a segment when its bounds do not overlap the filter's range. Always scan a segment with no bounds, so results cannot change.
5. Also read the `extract(epoch from now())` filter form that `lib/finelog/OPS.md` documents. Change `lib/finelog/OPS.md` to integer literals.

**Step 2: timestamp columns** (success 2 and 3)

6. Teach planning to read timestamp literals (`ts >= TIMESTAMP '...'`, `ts > now() - INTERVAL '1 hour'`). Planning ignores them today.
7. Set the flag on `iris.task`, `iris.worker`, `iris.profile` and `zephyr.worker`.

### Rollout

Each step deploys to `marin-dev`, then the three CoreWeave servers, then the hub. Each deploy is approved separately. Before the hub deploy, record a baseline of the issue's one-hour query.

### Expected Timeframe

- Step 1: about 1 week to a reviewed PR, then 1–2 days to deploy.
- Step 2: about 3 days to a reviewed PR, then 1 day to deploy.

### Alternatives Considered

| Option | Why not |
|---|---|
| **Leave it in place.** Add a `seq` range to time-bounded queries. | Works today, but a user must first find the `seq` range for a time. |
| **Larger footer and index caches.** | The hub reports show 12–36 footer reads for about 2,300 files and about 7,080 index cache hits: the caches were warm and the queries were still slow. A cache also empties at each restart and must grow with the table's history. |
| **Partition `log` by time.** | Finelog has no time transform, partition selection needs exact values (`=`, `IN`), and the query side does not read a table's own partition spec. A `day` column would change every writer and query and need a rewrite of about 325 GB. |
| **Make `epoch_ms` the key column of `log`.** | The `key` bounds make per-source reads (`key = ...`) fast, which is `log`'s main read path. Keeping `key` as the sort order would need an explicit sort setting, which is part of the source layout and so rewrites the table. |
