issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
Native SFTSpec Snowball d1024 training on one 8×H100 node passes forward evaluation but can hang in the first optimizer update. Every GPU reports 100% utilization, zero memory traffic and roughly 120–215W; Python rank main threads remain in XLA ExecuteReplicated. No completed update appears after more than five minutes. This blocks unmodified-runtime loss curves and throughput comparisons. d768 full-target training also stalled; d768 assistant-target and both d512 masks completed 20 updates.

Reproduce:
1. Load `open-athena/Snowflake-d1024-Base-262K-2026.10.19` at revision `dd3c5e3c156cfbe936fc0b59932c747e47c21d04` through native SFTSpec→TrainLmConfig→train_lm. Use sequence length 262144, global batch 8, microbatch 1, context parallel 4/data parallel 2, expert parallel 1, FP32 master parameters, BF16 computation, Sonic dispatch, gpu_fa4_cute attention, offloaded Muon-H optimizer and cuda_async allocator. The raw HF checkpoint evaluation and a second evaluation after resetting seven output-head token columns to fixed anchor columns both finish and match independently computed losses within 0.001. Training controls use assistant-only targets, data/trainer seed 0, sequential 262144-position packing and the pinned phase 0 Experiment 1 mixture. Its complete component paths, weights, reserved split and shuffle settings are in the consumed-config receipt linked below.
2. Use `XLA_FLAGS="--xla_gpu_shard_autotuning=false --xla_gpu_nccl_termination_timeout_seconds=600"` and execute the first backward/update. The local reproduction entry point is `experiments/post_training/snowball_isoflop/diagnostic.py`; source 33b69d10df preserves the isolated controls and later 97f6a242e6 exposes the explicit SFTSpec runtime field. These commits are local research commits, currently unpublished.
3. Compare the controls below, each starting from the same two-flag baseline in step 2. Baseline command-buffer and async-collective behavior is left at the JAX runtime default; neither has an extra override. Read-only inspection of a fresh campaign worker confirms jax, jaxlib, jax-cuda13-plugin and jax-cuda13-pjrt all 0.11.1. These match the GPU dependency pins used by the diagnostic source.

Expected: the first optimizer update completes, followed by finite training steps, without forced host launch synchronization.

| Runtime control | Observed result |
|---|---|
| Source async-collective runtime | First-update stall |
| Add `--xla_gpu_disable_async_collectives=ALLCOLLECTIVES` | First-update stall; NCCL collective counts agree across all ranks (AllGather 1460, ReduceScatter 99, AllReduce 46 globally) |
| Add only `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1` | First-update stall |
| Add only `--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=` | First-update stall |
| Both command buffers off and `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1` | 20 finite updates, permanent step 19 checkpoint, both initial-loss gates pass |
| Source runtime under Nsight Systems CUDA/NVTX tracing | 14 finite updates before deliberate bounded termination; CUDA graphs remain active |

The successful unprofiled joint control's first update took about 99 seconds; subsequent warm inclusive median 9.2473s/update, minimum unused allocator capacity 55.54% (the JAX allocator is limited to approximately 75% of physical GPU memory). One profiled run progressed while the unprofiled source-runtime attempt stalled; repeatability of this difference is not established. Its available trace contains 1,531,280 kernels across all 8 GPUs and 91,112 cuGraphLaunch calls. The report emitted a StringStorage processing warning, so exported events have that caveat. Successful completed kernels do not identify the operation stuck in unprofiled execution. NCCL 2.31.2, CUDA runtime 13.3, driver API 13.2 were reported. Agreement of NCCL counters in the synchronous-collective control does not prove which kernel or communication operation is responsible.

Preserved profile: `s3://marin-us-east-08a/marin/users/benfeuer/snowball-isoflop/2026.11.13.9/diagnostic-kernel-profile-d1024-assistant-seed0-n20/nsys/r00000-gb95de0.nsys-rep` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-08a%2Fmarin%2Fusers%2Fbenfeuer%2Fsnowball-isoflop%2F2026.11.13.9%2Fdiagnostic-kernel-profile-d1024-assistant-seed0-n20%2Fnsys%2Fr00000-gb95de0.nsys-rep)); exported summary is `analysis/kernel-summary.json` beside its nsys directory. Control directories in that same 2026.11.13.9 prefix are `calibration-d1024-assistant-seed0-n20` (source runtime), `diagnostic-serial-collectives-d1024-assistant-seed0-n20`, `diagnostic-launch-blocking-d1024-assistant-seed0-n20`, `diagnostic-no-command-buffer-d1024-assistant-seed0-n20`, and `diagnostic-synchronous-launches-d1024-assistant-seed0-n20`. Each preserves `consumed-config.json`, `dispatch.json` and initial-evaluation receipts. The complete successful joint-control config is [available in Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-08a%2Fmarin%2Fusers%2Fbenfeuer%2Fsnowball-isoflop%2F2026.11.13.9%2Fdiagnostic-synchronous-launches-d1024-assistant-seed0-n20%2Fconsumed-config.json). Config and profile access require Marin credentials; the local source commits are not yet a public standalone reproducer.

Exact isolated-control entry point, from the research checkout inside an 8-GPU Iris coordinator: `python -m experiments.post_training.snowball_isoflop.diagnostic --size 1024 --mask assistant --runtime synchronous-launches --h100-hour-limit 3 --run`. Replace the runtime value with `serial-collectives`, `launch-blocking` or `no-command-buffer` for the other controls. The coordinator must target cw-rno2a with interactive priority and 259200-second timeout.

Related investigations: #7110 (concurrent TVM-FFI invocation), #8870 (multi-rack ragged EP hang). This single-node CP4/data2 Sonic case has not been reduced to either mechanism.

Fresh six-cell calibration update (2026-11-14 02:51UTC): both d1024 masks with the joint runtime progressed beyond15 finite updates. All four source-runtime arms (d512 full/assistant and d768 full/assistant) passed both initial-loss gates but stalled in their first update for more than five minutes. Read-only samples of each rank main thread show ExecuteReplicated; all32GPUs report100% utilization, zero memory traffic and117–171W. The successful V9 d512/d768 assistant trajectories and these V10 stalls show that earlier small-size successes do not establish reliable source-runtime execution. The newer source adds token-count metric reductions relative to the original calibration; this is an attribution caveat, although CPU comparison verifies unchanged numerical training settings. All source-runtime failed-arm receipts remain under `2026.11.13.10/calibration-d{512,768}-{full,assistant}-seed0-n20/`; their scoped recovery uses separate `calibration-recovery-` identities.

Runtime-control update (2026-11-14 04:25UTC): command buffers off plus launch blocking completed20-update native calibrations for d768 full and both d1024 masks, but still stalled both d512 masks and d768 assistant. Adding `--xla_gpu_disable_async_collectives=ALLCOLLECTIVES` to that joint setting completed20 finite updates for BOTH d512 masks and BOTH d768 masks, with dual initial-loss gates, finished trackers, permanent step19 checkpoints and safe allocator headroom. These are scoped loss-curve workarounds; their timings are excluded from source-runtime throughput comparisons. The corresponding SFTSpec runtime implementation is in local research source3a38e030d0 (unpublished).

A source-runtime d1024 `ring_gather_combine` control at CP4/data2 also stalled at the first update. A late CUDA-GDB attachment timed out before kernel queries; the job later failed, so retain an intervention caveat and do not infer a particular blocked kernel. Its archived output is preserved at `s3://marin-us-east-08a/marin/users/benfeuer/snowball-isoflop/2026.11.13.10/diagnostic-ring-r2/debugger-outputs.tar.zst` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-08a%2Fmarin%2Fusers%2Fbenfeuer%2Fsnowball-isoflop%2F2026.11.13.10%2Fdiagnostic-ring-r2%2Fdebugger-outputs.tar.zst)).

A d512 assistant CP8/data1/Sonic/offload-true control using SOURCE runtime (neither extra compiler flags nor launch blocking) completed20 finite updates, both gates, permanent step19 and zero measured sender/receiver drops. Minimum allocator headroom80.19%; warm inclusive71,600 positions/s/GPU. Its supervisor recorded a rank0 cleanup segfault, although job, tracker and native checkpoint gates passed. All compared layout diagnostics use dispatch-count instrumentation, which differs from the main calibration and remains an attribution caveat. CP4/data2 offload-false was interrupted before training, so it does not establish an offload result. Geometry is a useful discriminator; a causal kernel mechanism remains unproven.

Batch-probe update (2026-11-14 04:35UTC): original SOURCE runtime also stalls d512, d768 and d1024 assistant-target CP4/data2/Sonic/offload-true probes at global batch2, microbatch1, accumulation1. All three pass both initial gates; none records an update more than9 minutes after the first batch is loaded. Read-only snapshots show all24GPUs at100% utilization and0% memory utilization, approximately118–217W. d512/d1024 main threads remain in ExecuteReplicated; d768 waits on ArrayImpl._value while reading the resulting loss scalar. Each stalled probe was stopped; total allocation6.64272H100-hours. These cells provide no valid throughput or batch-saturation measurements. Exact receipts are under `2026.11.13.10/B-accumulation-cp4-dp2-ep1-r1-sonic-offload1-mb1-acc1-grug_moe_muonh_v1-lr5e-05-d{512,768,1024}-assistant-seed0-n8/` beside the previous artifacts. This extends the observed failure beyond accumulation4/globalbatch8, without proving its cause.

The d1024 full-mask three-setting runtime (joint setting plus ALLCOLLECTIVES) also completed20 finite updates, both initial gates, finished tracking and a permanent step19 checkpoint. The matching assistant confirmation is running; uniform loss-phase runtime has not yet been selected from that pending result.

CP8 feasibility update (2026-11-14 04:59UTC): source-runtime batch8/microbatch1/accumulation8/Sonic/offload-true probes completed8 finite updates for d512 AND d768. Both have finished trackers, dual initial-loss gates, permanent step7 checkpoints and zero measured sender/receiver drops. Warm inclusive positions/s/GPU are48,324 and48,514; minimum allocator headroom81.20% and73.08%. Both supervisors killed rank0 during cleanup despite successful job/tracker/checkpoint gates. The d1024 CP8 cell passed both initial gates but stalled before its first update; two read-only samples several minutes apart show ExecuteReplicated and all8GPUs100% utilization/0% memory utilization/~118–130W. It was stopped after both smaller endpoints were verified. Thus CP8 is a positive discriminator for two sizes, not a universal recovery. All three use identical dispatch-count instrumentation and the original two E2 flags; no loss-phase runtime overrides.

The three-setting d1024 assistant confirmation also completed its first update and reached final native checkpoint/export, but its3-H100-hour bound interrupted export with only19 published training rows. It is not accepted as completed calibration and is not another first-update stall. A separate fresh4-hour confirmation preserves the interrupted artifacts and the full calibration requirements.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

The compiled training step computes gradients and applies the optimizer in one execution. The reported forward evaluations and runtime controls do not identify which operation stalls. Command buffers disabled together with `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1` completed 20 updates; each control alone stalled. One source-runtime run under Nsight reached 14 updates, but repeatability is unknown. The cited diagnostic commits `33b69d10df` and `97f6a242e6` are absent from this checkout and GitHub; the exact workload cannot yet be reproduced from published source. [#7110](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7110) and [#8870](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8870) involve different kernels or topologies and do not identify this stall.

**Relevant code**
- [`trainer.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/levanter/src/levanter/trainer.py#L726-L749) — gradients and optimizer share a compiled step.
- [`snowball.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/levanter/src/levanter/models/snowball.py#L430-L455) — Snowball attention dispatch.
- [`_fa4_cute.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_fa4_cute.py#L311-L335) — H100 attention backend.
- [`sonic.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/sonic.py#L248-L310) — Sonic dispatch and backward.
- [`muonh.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/levanter/src/levanter/optim/muonh.py#L54-L100) — Muon-H optimizer construction.

# Proposed Fix

1. Publish the isolated `diagnostic.py`, its SFTSpec runtime field, and exact dependency pins in a reviewable branch. Link its consumed-config receipt. Give every trial a first-update deadline and preserve its result and source revision.
2. On the same 8×H100 configuration, repeat the source runtime and passing joint control three times each. Run a separate traced source-runtime arm to measure the Nsight effect. Record per-rank progress, NCCL RAS, XLA executable dumps, and loaded CUDA/NCCL versions; stop each stalled trial after a 10-minute first-update deadline.
3. Split the first update at the gradient/optimizer boundary with the same parameters, batch, and mesh: evaluate gradients without applying them, then apply the optimizer to captured gradients. If gradients stall, replace FA4 and Sonic independently. Capture a GPU kernel/stream stack from a stalled rank before changing more runtime flags. These ablations localize a suspect; they do not by themselves prove a cause if recompilation changes launch order.
4. Fix the identified component in Marin or report a minimal reproducer upstream. Validate the original unprofiled runtime without launch synchronization across three cold 20-update runs, with finite losses, the existing initial-loss gates, and warm-step timing against the 9.2473 s joint-control median. Add a regression test for the isolated failure before opening a fix PR.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 Additional full-model reproduction on **64 H100 (8 nodes), Snowball/Grug 67B-A2B, d2560**: 26 layers, 256 experts/top-4, CP8/data8/EP1, sequence 262144, global batch 32, accumulation 4, Sonic + FA4 CuTe, JAX 0.11.1. Source pin: `0a4a1a6eab6ce979d67e1337b322eea3f1f83acd`. Recipe: Exp1 + per-group clip 1, BF16 stored, adam_lr 1:1; stage 0 only, offloaded optimizer state. The historical optimizer applies Muon-H to dense matrices, Adam to rank-4 expert banks and AdamH to output_proj.

All cases below already had command buffers disabled, shard autotuning disabled and the Iris autotune cache enabled.

| Case | LR | Runtime | Outcome |
|---|---:|---|---|
| r5b | 2e-5 | EAGER, autotune level 4 | One successful 25-update run. First execution 58.33 s; updates 2–5 mean 44.08 s. All 15 eval sets completed at updates 15 and 25 (token-weighted NLL 0.672724 / 0.660441). |
| r6, two arms | 5e-5 / 1e-4 | EAGER, autotune level 4 | Both stalled in the first execution after compilation; stopped at the 900 s first-step rule. Zero completed updates. |
| r7, two arms | 5e-5 / 1e-4 | EAGER, autotune level 4, plus CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1 and ALLCOLLECTIVES | Both stalled in the first execution; stopped at the 600 s rule. Zero completed updates. |
| r5c | 2e-5 | LAZY, autotune level 0; no launch-blocking/ALLCOLLECTIVES overrides | Seven finite updates before deliberate cancellation. About 120 s/update; update-15 eval was not reached. |

The r6 deadline captures covered all 64 ranks per arm: 51 and 52 of 64, respectively, main stacks included `cuModuleLoadData → jax::cuda::TritonKernelCall`. In r7, all 64 captured main stacks in each arm instead included `cuLaunchKernelEx → ncclLaunchKernel → ncclGroupEnd → xla::gpu::NcclGroupLaunch`. Sampled GPUs showed 100% SM utilization and 0% memory utilization.

For each r7 arm, NCCL RAS samples at 07:00:49Z and 07:02:35Z on 2026-11-14 had **all 170 matched communicator/collective min/max counter entries unchanged**, with no communicators added or lost. Thus there was no observed counter advance over approximately 106 s.

The three-setting workaround reported here at 8 H100 has not qualified at our 64-H100/full-model geometry. The successful r5b run also did not establish reliability. LR constants differ across the successful and stalled cases, and the stack/counter observations do not identify a unique causal kernel. The level 0 result establishes several completed updates, not a completed held-out-eval qualification.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖

A synthetic Snowball step stalled on one 8×H100 node with four layers, 8,192 tokens per sequence, CP4/DP2, and global batch 2. The probe used random weights and generated packed tokens. The reference-attention variant also reached the 16-minute timeout without completing step 0. A separate 262,144-token probe stalled while computing gradients, before the optimizer ran. [8K baseline](https://iris-cw-rno2a.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fdlwh%2Fsnowball-11440-synth-8k-4l) · [Reference attention](https://iris-cw-rno2a.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fdlwh%2Fsnowball-11440-reference-attn) · [Gradient split](https://iris-cw-rno2a.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fdlwh%2Fsnowball-11440-split-d512)

Adding `--xla_gpu_autotune_level=0` to the two XLA flags in the issue body let two fresh width-512 runs (batch 2) and one width-1024 run (batch 8) each finish 20 updates with finite loss on all eight ranks. They used JAX 0.11.1, NCCL 2.31.2, 262,144-token sequences, and a task-local compilation cache. CUDA launch and command-buffer settings used their defaults. [Width-512 repeat 1](https://iris-cw-rno2a.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fdlwh%2Fsnowball-11440-no-autotune-r2) · [Width-512 repeat 2](https://iris-cw-rno2a.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fdlwh%2Fsnowball-11440-no-autotune-r3) · [Width-1024](https://iris-cw-rno2a.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fdlwh%2Fsnowball-11440-d1024-no-autotune)

The investigation checkout exposes this setting as `--runtime no-autotune`. The original workload still needs a run that passes both initial-loss checks. Access to the reference values for those checks is pending. A JAX-only reproduction is still under investigation.


### JAX-only replay on 8×H100

A fresh JAX 0.11.1 process recompiles the captured StableHLO and calls PJRT directly. The graph uses reference attention, scatter dispatch, and XLA ragged dot. It contains zero StableHLO custom calls. The runner recreates the input buffers as zeros, so the replay needs only the graph, compiler options, and input shapes. No Marin, Levanter, or Triton Python package is required at replay time.

With the original flags, all eight ranks finished compilation and entered execution. The GPUs remained at 100% utilization with 0% reported memory utilization. All 35 NCCL counters stayed unchanged between two snapshots 108 seconds apart. The same fixture completed on all ranks with only `--xla_gpu_autotune_level=0` added. [Original flags](https://iris-cw-rno2a.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fdlwh%2Fsnowball-11440-jax-portable-stock) · [Autotuning disabled](https://iris-cw-rno2a.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fdlwh%2Fsnowball-11440-jax-portable-level0)

This reproduces the stall signature in the JAX/XLA GPU stack. The exact deadlock and its relationship to the original training run still need localization.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖

A captured StableHLO training step compiles on all eight ranks, then stalls during execution with the original XLA flags in NVIDIA JAX Toolbox's November 16, 2026 nightly. Adding `--xla_gpu_autotune_level=0` lets every rank complete.

The graph comes from a four-layer, 8,192-token synthetic Snowball training step with reference attention, scatter dispatch, and XLA ragged dot. It contains zero StableHLO custom calls. The runner imports Python standard-library modules, JAX, jaxlib, and NumPy and calls PJRT directly. It creates 203 input buffers filled with zeros. The test measures execution completion. Replay requires no model checkpoint, dataset, Marin installation, or storage credentials.

Use one Linux x86-64 host with eight NVIDIA H100 80 GB GPUs and NVIDIA Container Toolkit. The observed runs used driver 595.71.05, 32 CPUs, and a 384 GiB host-memory limit. This fixture is an eight-process replay, with one GPU per process.

The pinned image is `ghcr.io/nvidia/jax@sha256:87178492d5b1bb56c32efd039f40de3913e507f675eec522b89affb697838314`. It reports JAX `0.12.1.dev20261116+a9797b362b`, jaxlib `0.12.1.dev20261116`, and NCCL `2.32.3`. NCCL RAS reports CUDA runtime and driver API version `13040`. The image was built at `2026-11-16T15:40:46Z` from JAX Toolbox revision `dd737d099a8f85a4743663ee1cecb9e8040c0ba4`.

The complete standalone fixture, runner, and sanitized NCCL counter snapshots are public in [this Gist](https://gist.github.com/dlwh/ae4f8156427e940594d2d768aeaa3491/3900c478c333a6ebfd69d2d15c300211b1f06e9f). Clone it and check out the pinned revision.

```bash
git clone https://gist.github.com/ae4f8156427e940594d2d768aeaa3491.git snowball-11440-repro
cd snowball-11440-repro
git checkout 3900c478c333a6ebfd69d2d15c300211b1f06e9f
```

Decode the graph and verify its SHA-256. Run every command below from this directory.

```bash
base64 --decode module.mlirbc.gz.b64 | gzip --decompress > module.mlirbc
echo 'b3cd3501c0b1edf3334fad9130562419c15a7aed7d58877eedf3970820859cb6  module.mlirbc' | sha256sum --check
```

Define the launcher in the same shell. It overrides the image's default XLA_FLAGS, matching the Iris runs, and leaves command buffers, async collectives, and CUDA launch synchronization at runtime defaults.

```bash
IMAGE='ghcr.io/nvidia/jax@sha256:87178492d5b1bb56c32efd039f40de3913e507f675eec522b89affb697838314'
BASE_FLAGS='--xla_gpu_shard_autotuning=false --xla_gpu_nccl_termination_timeout_seconds=600'

replay() {
  docker run --rm --gpus all --ipc=host \
    --ulimit memlock=-1 --ulimit stack=67108864 \
    --memory=384g --cpus=32 \
    --mount "type=bind,src=$PWD,dst=/repro,readonly" --workdir /repro \
    --env JAX_PLATFORMS=cuda,cpu \
    --env XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false \
    --env NCCL_DEBUG=INFO --env NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=INIT,ALLOC \
    --env "XLA_FLAGS=$1" --entrypoint /bin/bash "$IMAGE" -c \
    'python -I -c "import jax, jaxlib; print(jax.__version__, jaxlib.__version__, flush=True)" &&
     exec timeout --kill-after=15s 840s python -I jax_replay.py . --generate-inputs --port 43767'
}
```

Run the original flags, then the control. Run these separately so the control still runs if the first command returns a timeout status.

```bash
replay "$BASE_FLAGS"
```

```bash
replay "$BASE_FLAGS --xla_gpu_autotune_level=0"
```

Correct execution would print `execution complete` on every rank and exit 0. To reproduce the reported failure, the original-flags command should instead stall and time out with status 124. The autotuning-disabled control should complete on all eight ranks and exit 0. These expectations come from the observed comparison, which used the identical image, graph, launcher inputs, host-memory allocation, and preallocation setting in separate Iris/Kubernetes jobs. The Docker command above is the portable equivalent of those runs and has not itself been executed.

| Setting | Observed result |
|---|---|
| Original XLA flags | Every rank compiled in 323–351 seconds and entered execution. Zero ranks completed before the command's 840-second total timeout. Task exit 124. |
| Add only `--xla_gpu_autotune_level=0` | Every rank completed execution in 14.32–21.26 seconds after its execution marker. Task exit 0. |

In the original-flags run, GPU utilization sampled at multiple points was 0% on every GPU, with about 14–18 GiB allocated per GPU. All 24 matched communicator/rank collective-counter entries stayed unchanged between NCCL RAS snapshots at 19:03:37Z and 19:05:03Z on November 16. The two `nccl-counters-*.json` files preserve those counters with host identities and PIDs removed. These observations establish a bounded execution stall. Sampling can miss intermittent activity, and the specific blocked operation is unresolved.

Earlier runs at a 64 GiB host-memory limit were OOM-killed during compilation. At 384 GiB with default GPU preallocation, both autotuning settings compiled but encountered CUDA OOM in `ncclCommSplit`. The comparison above uses `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false` for both runs and avoids that OOM.

A JAX 0.11.1 replay of the same fixture also timed out with the original flags and completed with autotuning disabled. Its stalled GPUs reported 100% utilization and 0% memory utilization. Whether the old and new runtime stalls share a cause is unresolved.

- [Marin issue #11440](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11440)
- [November 16 nightly, original flags](https://iris-cw-rno2a.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fdlwh%2Fsnowball-11440-toolbox-stock-no-prealloc)
- [November 16 nightly, autotuning disabled](https://iris-cw-rno2a.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fdlwh%2Fsnowball-11440-toolbox-level0-no-prealloc)
- [JAX 0.11.1, original flags](https://iris-cw-rno2a.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fdlwh%2Fsnowball-11440-jax-portable-stock)
- [JAX 0.11.1, autotuning disabled](https://iris-cw-rno2a.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fdlwh%2Fsnowball-11440-jax-portable-level0)

The Iris dashboards require Marin access. The files in the linked Gist and the commands above are sufficient for an independent replay. Compilation and execution can perturb timing, and a broader reliability study has not been performed.

The runner and captured graph originate from the Apache-2.0-licensed Marin project. The exact StableHLO file hash above identifies the fixture used in the observed runs.

issues.title: [levanter] Snowball stalls in the first H100 optimizer update

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
## TL;DR

Snowball (10/05 SFT) often writes broken JSON for Pi's nested `edit` tool call, and the episode ends there. In an RL pass-rate screen (128 SWE-smith tasks × 8 tries, Pi 0.87.0), 575 of 1,024 tries ended on a malformed call. 524 of the 576 malformed spans were `edit` calls. The SFT data contains almost no calls in Pi's nested edit shape. Plan: add a slice of valid nested edits to SFT and measure the malformed-edit rate.

## Description

Pi's edit tool takes `{"path": …, "edits": [{"oldText": …, "newText": …}, …]}`, a list of objects inside the arguments object. The 10/05 SFT data has about 2.7M flat `str_replace_editor(command, path, old_str, new_str)` calls and essentially no Pi-shape edits.

Measured in the screen above:
- 1,093 edit calls; 523 failed `json.loads`.
- 362 of the 524 broken edit spans parse after one insertion at the JSON error offset: `]}` for 259, `}` for 103. This is a syntax-only check. It does not show that the repaired edit applies or fixes the task.
- 14 of the 575 broken-call tries still scored 1, so a malformed final call does not always mean a failed task.

Examples are viewable in the eval trace viewer (Marina login required): https://applets.marina.oa.dev/a/943a733c-1d78-4b3b-8d7c-060aefb8726e/, run "Pass-rate 43604". Missing `]}`: attempts `010d96c8bd03428fb13da34e880a3a73` (step 18) and `0288247ea31c47e48cbb5c7ee3b6a467` (step 11). Missing `}`: `04741406ca5a4ff38401423e48ccd4ad` (step 18).

An A/B with a flat replacement edit tool (16 tasks × 2 arms × 4 tries) solved 20/64 vs 7/64 for Pi's native tool. Malformed calls not caused by the output cap were 3 vs 25. A larger confirmation (128 tasks × 8 per arm) is pending review. Third-party harnesses fix their own tool schemas, so a flat tool would only help our own harness.

The SFT training data's tool calls are well-formed: 452 of 47,399,691 assistant call spans failed a delimiter and `json.loads` check, across 51 scanned sources.

## Hypothesis or Goal

The model learned the flat edit shape in SFT and miscounts brackets in Pi's nested shape. Adding valid nested-edit calls to SFT should cut the malformed-edit rate without lowering other scores.

## Status

- E12-B data built: 1,000 train / 100 val / 100 test synthetic Pi edit exercises from TMax code (ODC-BY), 1–4 edits per call, 393,750 supervised tokens in train. Each edit was checked to restore the target file exactly. [Manifest](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Flong-loop-436%2Fe12%2Farm-b-20261114-r1%2Fmanifest-r1.json) (`s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/long-loop-436/e12/arm-b-20261114-r1/manifest-r1.json`).
- 1 h version: three 15-update arms (general-only control, E12 full, E12 attention/head only) trained, exported and scored on Micro210. Results below.
- 8 h version: C150 recipe plus a grown E12-B set (~6k rows, at most 4 passes per row, about 0.8% of supervised tokens), against the existing C150 arm. It waits for the 1 h readout.
- Mochi: in its BFCL ×5 Pi traces, 1,445 tool calls parsed, and at most 3 messages left tool-call-like text unparsed. BFCL rarely uses `edit` (7 calls, none with more than one edit), so this does not test the nested-edit problem.

Readout: malformed-edit rate on Micro210's Pi trials, the Micro210 score paired by task, and the retention panel. Carry the slice into the next SFT stage if the malformed-edit rate falls by at least half against the matched control with no Micro210 or retention loss.

## Results (1 h version, as of 2026-11-17)

All three arms start from the 10/05 weights and run 15 updates of 32 × 262,144 tokens. In the two edit arms, the E12-B slice is 0.68% of supervised tokens: all 1,000 train exercises, seen twice. All Micro210 numbers are single runs; two runs of the parent differ by about 5 tasks (2.1 points).

| Model | Micro210, equal weight over 20 sources | vs parent run 1 | Held-out E12 edit loss (100 test rows, update 15) | Malformed `edit` spans in Micro210 Pi traces (about 100 records; one outlier record excluded) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10/05 parent, run 1 / repeat | 49.39 / 47.32 | 0 / −2.1 | not measured | 16 |
| General-only control | 43.57 | −5.8 | 0.0294 | 14 |
| E12 attention + head only | 46.52 | −2.9 | 0.0294 | 20 |
| E12 full | 42.48 | −6.9 | 0.0018 | 3 |

- **The control loses about as much as the full arm**, so the Micro210 drop comes from the continued training itself, not from the edit data. One untested difference: E12 restarted at LR 2e-5 with fresh optimizer moments, while 10/05 ended its decay at 5e-6. A rerun of the control at 5e-6 and a zero-update export control are being prepared.
- **The edit data taught the format only when all weights trained.** The full arm's held-out edit loss is 16× lower than the control's. The attention + head arm did not change.
- **Not shown yet:** that real edits improved. The malformed counts are witness counts, not rates. The excluded full-arm record alone holds 8,166 malformed spans (see the comment of 2026-11-17 07:34 UTC). A behavioral test is being built: each model answers the 100 held-out test prompts, and the returned edit is applied with Pi's edit function and checked against the target file.
- The pre-stated carry rule (malformed-edit rate at least halved, with no Micro210 or retention loss) is **not met**: the full arm loses 6.9 points.

## Links

* Logbook:
* W&B Report:
* Important updates:

## Decision Log

- 2026-11-16: Do not train on the screen's own successful calls; those tasks are the readout panels.
- 2026-11-16: Keep Pi's native edit tool for reported benchmarks.

## Conclusion

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 **Protocol FAIL; original preregistered confirmation claim FALSE.** The run completed, but the strict tool-contract check failed. The numbers below are descriptive, not a confirmed flat-edit effect or a promotion decision.

We compared Pi’s native nested edit arguments with a flat replacement on the same 128 SWE-smith training tasks, eight attempts per arm: 2,048 assignments. There were 2,024 verified binary outcomes and 24 masked/unknown outcomes, which were not counted as failures.

| Descriptive reading | Control wins / known | Flat wins / known | Complete task profiles | Flat-minus-control task-profile difference | Conditional 95% interval |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| As recorded | 161 / 1,011 | 307 / 1,013 | 120 | **+14.38 percentage points** | +10.21 to +18.85 |
| Two affected attempts excluded | 161 / 1,011 | 305 / 1,011 | 118 | **+14.30 percentage points** | +9.96 to +18.75 |

The second reading removes two verified flat-arm wins from the pooled sensitivity only: nominal denominators become 1,024 control and 1,022 flat. The 13 control and 11 flat unknowns remain unknown. For the separate balanced eight-per-arm task comparison, the two affected task profiles become incomplete and are omitted; their other 30 outcomes remain pooled. The original endpoint is unchanged. These intervals condition on the observed complete task profiles; they do not cover excluded-task uncertainty, shared-run dependence, training-repeat variation or population generalization.

**Why strict confirmation failed:** two flat-arm attempts contained 65 requests using the native nested edit schema. Contracts were checked in 1,015 attempts per arm: zero affected control attempts and two affected flat attempts. Unchecked attempts and incomplete guard exposure are not assumed clean.

**Supported explanation:** in both cases, the outer agent ran `pi submit` through its bash tool. Pi 0.87 treats `submit` as a prompt, not a submission command. The resulting recorded requests use the default native tools; the outer flat extension was supplied through explicit CLI flags that the child commands omitted. The parent’s flat requests resume afterward with its prior context preserved. Pinned source and retained command/request/tool-result ordering support a recursive CLI invocation explanation, rather than an established parent compaction switch. Captured OS ancestry, every child setting/binary, original HTTP traffic and the effect of those calls on reward were not proved. This explanation does not repair the protocol failure.

Independent review reproduced the archive/grid joins, counts, bootstrap intervals and both sensitivities. Cost was **26.20 requested H100-hours**, not a utilization or invoice measurement. Native jobs and containers completed; exact GPU Pod absence/provider release has not yet been established. No new run, harness change or training-data promotion follows from this result.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 Mochi nested-edit screen: the frozen test ended undecided (coverage hold). It shows neither "slice needed" nor "no slice needed". The descriptive numbers, over selected evidence-complete pairs and retained returned spans, are much lower for Mochi than for Snowball, but they cannot decide the 5% line.

## Result

The screen ran Mochi SFT step 400407 on the same 128 SWE-smith tasks × 8 tries as the Snowball pass-rate screen. Setup: Pi 0.87.0, the nested `edit` tool, one DP16 GB200 serve in cw-us-east-08a, 32 trials at once, a 900 s agent cap and no retries.

The frozen rule sorts each of the 1,024 assigned pairs into one of three classes:
- BAD: a broken tool-call body under a verified request contract.
- CLEAN: fully recorded, no broken call, and a clean ending.
- UNKNOWN: everything else.

It decides "slice" at 205 BAD and "no slice" at 973 CLEAN.

| Run (same 128 tasks × 8, same readout code) | BAD / CLEAN / UNKNOWN of 1,024 | Frozen result | Agent timeouts (of readable) | Evidence-complete pairs (of readable) | Broken call / evidence-complete | Broken **edit** first / evidence-complete | Broken returned spans |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Snowball SFT `grug-datakit-sft-262k-20261005-ac60d940-r1` (run 43604; finished historical run) | 575 / 317 / 132 | same rule applied retrospectively: B ≥ 205 | 19 / 1,016 (1.9%) | 892 / 1,016 (87.8%) | 64.5% (61.3–67.5) | 58.7% (55.5–61.9) | 582 / 35,041 (1.66%); edit 524 / 1,093 |
| Mochi SFT step 400407 (stopped early) | 19 / 147 / 858 | undecided (coverage hold) | 289 / 464 (62.3%) | 166 / 464 (35.8%) | 11.4% (7.5–17.2) | 3.6% (1.7–7.7) | 22 / 10,040 (0.22%); edit 7 / 358 |

## Stop

At 06:15Z we declared a value stop: after the second interim look, continue only if B ≥ 100. That look had B = 18. We cancelled the screen at about 06:42Z, with 469 of 1,024 attempts recorded. This stop rule is separate from the frozen rule, and every unfinished pair counts as UNKNOWN.

## How to read it

- The Snowball row reruns the same frozen code on run 43604's retained traces. Its 575 BAD tries are exactly the 575 reported above. It is a finished historical run, not a complete capture: 132 pairs are UNKNOWN.
- Mochi's UNKNOWN pairs are 555 assigned pairs with no retained attempt record, 171 unmappable records, 124 incomplete request/turn records, 3 timeout endings and 5 unreadable records.
- No-slice was out of reach once the timeouts piled up. A timed-out try can never be CLEAN under the frozen rule, and 289 timeouts alone cap CLEAN at 735.
- The intervals are nominal 95% Wilson intervals over each run's evidence-complete pairs. They do not account for which tries finished or for dependence within a task, and they are not calibrated for the 1,024. Mochi's evidence-complete pairs contain no timed-out try, so they may lean towards shorter episodes.
- The span column counts broken tool-call bodies among the calls the model returned, using lexical tool names. It is not a prevalence of executed calls.
- The runs differ in model and serve, so this table compares descriptions and does not give a causal effect.

## Timeout-aware sensitivity

This was declared after the first look and is descriptive only. It checks the proved prefix of each timed-out try for a broken call. It found none in the 289 eligible timeouts, so the witness count stays at 19 of 1,024.

## Cost

76.07 GB200-hours over six serve starts, from Iris task durations × 4 GB200 per task. The CPU-only screen drivers are not included. The total uses unrounded durations; the rounded rows below sum to 76.08.

| Start | GB200-h |
|---|---:|
| r1 | 2.86 |
| r2 | 9.21 |
| r3 | 3.61 |
| r4 | 1.01 |
| r5 | 3.01 |
| r6 | 56.38 |

r5's serve was ready, but its screen failed at worker start-up: the local-machine factory found bubblewrap blocked on that CPU pod (see issue 10692).

## Follow-up

What a cleaner Mochi test could try (hypotheses; nothing built):
- A longer agent cap, to test whether more attempts finish and satisfy the capture checks.
- Higher trial concurrency, for better use of the serve. In the run's first 35 minutes, mean inter-token latency was 141 ms (about 7 tok/s per sequence) at 32 concurrent trials. Higher concurrency may slow each sequence further, and it is not shown to improve completions.

Two retained-trace snapshots, taken about 15 minutes apart after the stop, agree exactly. That is an observation, not proof of final retention. Private traces are not published. Leftover Daytona sandboxes were not observed; they were created with a 360-minute lifetime.

issues.body:
🤖 Curated Python code evaluations fail every attempt during grading with `Grading environment setup failed: exit=1`. The model's responses are fine, but no sample is scored. This affects HumanEval+, MBPP+ and CRUXEval on current main.

The code graders declare `python3 /tests/prepare.py` as an environment setup command ([`convert_python`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/importers/evalchemy/code.py)). `prepare.py` reads the candidate's answer from `/app/answer.txt` to build the test program. [`_grade_on`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/runtime/grading.py) runs setup commands before it installs the submission archive that contains `/app/answer.txt`, so `prepare.py` fails:

```
File "/tests/prepare.py", line 15, in main
    response = Path("/app/answer.txt").read_text()
FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '/app/answer.txt'
```

Reproduce:
1. Run a curated `cruxeval`, `humanevalplus` or `mbppplus` evaluation from main.
2. Read `data/evaluation_attempts` in the run's results. Every finished attempt has `outcome = infra_error`, and its result blob carries the traceback above in `grade.diagnostics.stderr`.

Expected: the code graders can read the candidate's answer, either because the answer is installed before `prepare.py` runs or because preparation runs after the submission is installed.

Observed in CRUXEval run `20261113-192007-Qwen-Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-2c59e4d3702e48eab27ff3b1ddbe5c60-cruxeval-dda752051d0a55b3a9b6706ffcd6a9fe`, where every attempt on all 20 smoke items failed this way. HumanEval+ and MBPP+ use the same setup command; I have not run them yet.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

`convert_python` puts `prepare.py` in environment setup, but `_grade_on` installs the answer archive after setup. The runtime order is intentional: a candidate file must be able to replace a setup fixture. PR #10115 changes grading failure classification in the same runtime file but does not address this recipe.

**Relevant code**
- [`code.py#L103-L130`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/importers/evalchemy/code.py#L103-L130) — Python grader recipe.
- [`grading.py#L621-L650`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/runtime/grading.py#L621-L650) — setup precedes answer installation.
- [`test_runtime.py#L911-L930`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/taskcompendium/tests/test_runtime.py#L911-L930) — setup fixture replacement contract.

# Proposed Fix

Run `prepare.py` immediately before `program.py` in the Python grader command, after the answer archive is installed. Advance the code recipe revision and check the published grader recipe in a regression test.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body: 🤖 Fix proposed in #11408. It runs Python code preparation after answer staging and advances CODE_REVISION. Eight focused TaskCompendium tests pass; the affected runner's Harbor `os.pidfd_open` failure reproduces on unmodified main. The live evaluation suites have not been rerun.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body: 🤖 Fresh production evidence from the Atlas difficulty v17 rounds (2026-11-17): the four Evalchemy code graders (cruxeval, humaneval, humanevalplus, mbppplus) burned 600+ infrastructure attempts each — every attempt, valid submission or not, because `python3 /tests/prepare.py` runs as a setup command (`importers/evalchemy/code.py` line 113) and the submission archive (which carries `/app/answer.txt`) installs only after setup (`runtime/grading.py::_grade_on`). Repro: grade any of these sources with the small-solver campaign; the grading environment setup fails with `FileNotFoundError: /app/answer.txt` inside the rebuilt task-curation env image. Fix landed on `atlas-env-audit` as 1ecadd3fdb ('Stage script-grader submissions before setup commands run'): for script graders with an answer path the submission archive installs before setup too; the post-setup install still runs, preserving replace-afterward semantics for setups that write fixtures at the answer path. Behavioral tests in `lib/taskcompendium/tests/test_script_grader.py`.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
Iris task resource rows leave accelerator utilization and memory fields null, which prevents resource comparisons between trainer and inference tasks.

Reproduce:
1. Run a GPU task on a Kubernetes Iris cluster with DCGM metrics available.
2. Query its rows in `iris.task`, selecting `accelerator_util_pct` and `accelerator_mem_bytes`.
3. Compare them with the node GPU telemetry and task GPU assignment for the same time window.
4. Observe null task fields even when node GPU samples exist.

Expected: task rows contain measurements attributed to the task's assigned GPUs when coverage is available; unsupported or missing coverage remains null.

Main `f5d3c85f9e` declares both fields in `IrisTaskStat`. The Kubernetes task-resource collector calls `build_task_stat` without either accelerator argument, so both default to null. Node GPU collection is a separate path. Observed GB200 samples had node GPU telemetry but null task accelerator fields. The required per-GPU-to-task attribution is absent from this collector.

No fix commit is prepared.

Example query (replace the task ID and use a bounded time window):
```sql
SELECT task_id, ts, accelerator_util_pct, accelerator_mem_bytes
FROM "iris.task"
WHERE task_id = '/OWNER/JOB/0'
  AND ts >= '2026-11-17T16:00:00' AND ts < '2026-11-17T16:30:00'
ORDER BY ts
```
Source: [Kubernetes task-resource collector](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f5d3c85f9e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/node_agent/kubernetes.py#L320). Node readings come from DCGM; task attribution must use the assigned GPU identities, with units and multi-GPU aggregation documented.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

`ResourceCollector.collect_once()` writes `iris.task` from metrics-server CPU and memory samples; its tracked state contains only task/attempt IDs and pod names. The separate node agent parses DCGM readings by GPU UUID and publishes node telemetry, but no path carries those readings or the pod's assigned GPU UUIDs into the task-row writer. A GPU count or node name cannot identify the assigned devices when tasks share a node. I found no open PR for #11613 or DCGM task attribution.

**Relevant code**
- [`tasks.py#L1834-L1902`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L1834-L1902) — task row collector
- [`tasks.py#L3135-L3156`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L3135-L3156) — running-pod registration
- [`kubernetes.py#L351-L449`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/node_agent/kubernetes.py#L351-L449) — per-GPU DCGM parsing
- [`metrics.py#L109-L127`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/node_agent/metrics.py#L109-L127) — GPU UUID telemetry
- [`controller.py#L309-L365`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/k8s/controller.py#L309-L365) — node-agent deployment

# Proposed Fix

1. Check a bounded H100 and GB200 DCGM scrape for pod/container labels and confirm whether those labels reliably identify the exact GPU UUIDs allocated to each pod. If they do not, use the node-local kubelet PodResources device IDs as the allocation source; the node-agent DaemonSet will need access to that socket.
2. Produce timestamped, per-pod GPU snapshots keyed by pod UID and GPU UUID. Carry them to the Kubernetes `ResourceCollector` through a bounded cluster-local interface, and join them to its existing CPU/memory rows by pod UID and attempt. Do not infer assignment from node totals or GPU request counts.
3. Set `accelerator_util_pct` to the mean utilization of all assigned GPUs and `accelerator_mem_bytes` to the sum of their used framebuffer bytes (DCGM MiB converted to bytes). Keep each field null when its assigned-device coverage is incomplete or stale; define the freshness bound against the collector's 15-second cadence.
4. Add behavior tests for two pods sharing a node, a multi-GPU pod, reassignment after pod restart, partial DCGM coverage, and a CPU-only pod. Verify a short live GPU task against the assigned UUIDs and `iris.task` rows before rollout.

This crosses the node agent, allocation discovery, and the task-row writer, so it needs a design and integration pass before a PR.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
Snowball training fails on its first forward pass because the Grug provider does not apply its per-layer context-parallel communication settings to non-Hero variants.

Reproduce:
1. Construct Snowball's `GrugModelProvider` through `GrugMoeBridge` with context parallelism 4, PP2, TP1, 26 layers, a 2048-token sliding window, and Snowball's configured global-layer pattern.
2. Leave communication selection to the provider defaults.
3. Run a training forward with Transformer Engine.
4. Observe `AssertionError: Context parallelism does not support sliding window attention with cp_comm_type='p2p'!`.

Expected: the provider selects supported communication modes for each layer and rejects incompatible explicit overrides before allocation.

Main `f5d3c85f9e` guards the per-layer settings with `provider.grug_hero` in `vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/models/grug_megatron_bridge.py`. Preflight accepted the intended mixed modes, but the runtime provider used the parent p2p default. The repair passed a provider regression and a four-GPU output/gradient parity probe. No attention-window or topology change was needed.

Source: [Grug bridge communication settings](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f5d3c85f9e/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/models/grug_megatron_bridge.py#L229).

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research
`GrugMoeBridge.provider_bridge()` computes Snowball's local/global layer pattern but assigns `cp_comm_type` only for Hero configs. Snowball therefore inherits Megatron's `p2p` default under CP4, which Transformer Engine rejects on sliding-window layers. The worker can overwrite `cp_comm_type` after bridge creation, so validation must inspect the final provider setting.

**Relevant code**
- [bridge lines 216–232](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7e6db4032f7ca69097b0c07603211ae70c801461/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/models/grug_megatron_bridge.py#L216-L232) — layer pattern and Hero-only communication
- [worker lines 158–175](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7e6db4032f7ca69097b0c07603211ae70c801461/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/workers/megatron/megatron_worker.py#L158-L175) — provider overrides and finalization

# Proposed Fix
`AutoBridge.from_hf_config()` reaches `GrugMoeBridge.provider_bridge()`, then worker overrides reach `GrugModelProvider.provide()` before model construction. Set the mixed modes for every Grug variant and reject CP>1 overrides that select a non-`a2a` mode on sliding-window layers before allocation.

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
**A higher-priority multi-host job cannot get capacity when a reservation is fully held by smaller, lower-priority slices.** Preemption only replaces one existing slice of the same size or larger. The autoscaler never scales down busy lower-priority slices to make room. So the job waits indefinitely, whatever its priority.

## Example (2026-11-17, reserved v4 pool, us-central2-b)

- **Demand:** a production-band (band 1) coscheduled job needing a v4-1024 slice (512 chips, 128 hosts), submitted 17:13Z.
  - Its scale group created a queued resource at 17:16:21Z. That resource was still `WAITING_FOR_RESOURCES` in GCP at 18:45Z.
  - All 128 tasks were pending with "No workers match constraints".
- **Supply:** the reservation's 1,024 chips were all in READY slices, every one running tasks. No slice was idle.

| Slice size | Ready slices | Chips | Bands of running tasks |
|---|---|---|---|
| v4-8 | 96 | 384 | batch (95), interactive (1) |
| v4-32 | 4 | 64 | batch, interactive |
| v4-64 | 4 | 128 | batch, interactive |
| v4-128 | 1 | 64 | batch |
| v4-256 | 1 | 128 | batch, interactive |
| v4-512 | 1 | 256 | batch |

- Every running task was in a lower band than the waiting job, yet nothing could be evicted for it.
- Removing about 512 chips of the smaller slices (for example most v4-8 slices plus the v4-128 and v4-256) would have let GCP create the v4-1024 slice.

## Why, in the code (main at f5d3c85f9e)

- **[`_preempt_coscheduled`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f5d3c85f9e4914a48994d9a29f8c3e9104de84e0/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/scheduling/policy.py#L456-L502)** evicts **one** victim slice. That slice must have the same `device_variant` as the preemptor, strictly lower band on every member, and at least `n_required` members. Smaller slices of another variant never qualify, and several slices are never combined.
- **[`run_preemption_pass`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f5d3c85f9e4914a48994d9a29f8c3e9104de84e0/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/scheduling/policy.py#L614-L637)** documents the same rule: a coscheduled preemptor evicts an entire slice "of the same device-variant and at least the preemptor's task count".
- **[`_preempt_coscheduled_partial_hosts`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f5d3c85f9e4914a48994d9a29f8c3e9104de84e0/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/scheduling/policy.py#L550-L565)** frees hosts by evicting solo co-tenants, but only on hosts of the gang's own variant, so it needs those workers to exist first.
- **Autoscaler scale-down is idle-based only** ([`scaling_group.py` idle threshold](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f5d3c85f9e4914a48994d9a29f8c3e9104de84e0/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/autoscaler/scaling_group.py#L125-L135)).
  - Routing orders groups by the group's config priority ([`route_demand`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f5d3c85f9e4914a48994d9a29f8c3e9104de84e0/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/autoscaler/routing.py#L715-L725)), not by the priority band of the demand.
  - Nothing releases busy lower-band slices to free reservation quota for higher-band demand that a group cannot satisfy.

The rule is deliberate: "same-variant + slice-shaped" avoids large/small thrashing. But inside a fixed reservation, it means priority cannot reclaim capacity that has been fragmented into smaller slices.

## Proposed direction

When a higher-band demand stays unmet because its group cannot get capacity in a reservation, the autoscaler should drain lower-band slices in the **same reservation** until enough chips are free for the requested slice:
- Preempt their tasks through the normal preemption path, then delete the slices.
- Prefer the lowest band, then the youngest tasks.
- Gate it on the demand having been unmet for a minimum time, and stop as soon as the chips are free, to limit thrashing.
- Record each drain (preemptor, victims, chips freed) so it can be audited.

---

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

The current preemption pass binds a coscheduled preemptor to workers freed by one same-variant slice, so it cannot combine smaller v4 slices into a new v4-1024 allocation. The autoscaler routes by scale-group priority, does not carry the pending job's band in `DemandEntry`, and scales down only idle slices; `quota_pool` groups quota failures but has no shared chip ledger. [#6818](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/6818) and [#6819](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/6819) developed the ledger, drain lifecycle, and cross-variant pass, then closed unmerged after inactivity. I found no open PR for this issue or mechanism.

**Relevant code**
- [`policy.py#L460-L503`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/scheduling/policy.py#L460-L503) — one same-variant victim slice
- [`models.py#L29-L39`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/autoscaler/models.py#L29-L39) — demand lacks priority band
- [`routing.py#L710-L756`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/autoscaler/routing.py#L710-L756) — group-priority routing
- [`scaling_group.py#L647-L671`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/autoscaler/scaling_group.py#L647-L671) — detach before cloud deletion
- [`controller.py#L1021-L1072`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/controller.py#L1021-L1072) — schedule and autoscale tick ordering

# Proposed design

A production v4-1024 demand should reclaim enough chips from lower-band slices in its own reserved pool, then wait for a new v4-1024 slice to become ready. This crosses scheduling, autoscaling, slice persistence, and cloud deletion, so I would split it into reviewable stages:

1. **Pool accounting and safe drain lifecycle.** Add an explicit physical chip budget to each reserved `quota_pool` (1,024 chips for the reported `v4-reserved/us-central2-b` pool), validate that all member groups agree, and derive a per-tick ledger of live, capacity-backed creating, and draining chips. Track `WAITING_FOR_RESOURCES` requests separately because they have not acquired chips. Keep a slice tracked as `DRAINING` until cloud deletion is confirmed; make drain idempotent and retry a stuck deletion. The autoscaler must count draining chips as unavailable for new allocations and cap launches across *all* sizes in the pool. Adapt the useful parts of #6818 to the current controller.
2. **Band-aware demand and cross-size drain.** Carry the requested priority band into `DemandEntry` and admit pool launches in band order. On an autoscale tick, when a reserved-pool demand has waited at least a configurable grace period and no ready or capacity-backed creating slice of the requested shape can satisfy it, calculate the chip deficit. A queued GCP resource still `WAITING_FOR_RESOURCES` must remain eligible for a drain; reuse that request after capacity is freed. Select physical victim slices in the same pool whose *every* occupant is strictly lower band, preferring the lowest band and then youngest tasks. Skip victims with a coscheduled job spanning several slices unless its whole gang can be handled. Evict nothing unless eligible victims cover the full deficit; stop selecting as soon as they do. Commit task preemption and slice drain together on the same tick, then launch or unblock the requested shape only after GCP releases the chips. Adapt #6819's physical-slice grouping and schedule-only-tick guard; include an audit record with preemptor, victims, pool, and chips freed.
3. **Regression and rollout gates.** Use a 1,024-chip mixed-size fixture matching this issue to prove that one production v4-1024 demand reclaims exactly enough lower-band chips and eventually receives its slice. Cover equal/higher-band occupants, another pool or zone, insufficient eligible chips, a queued replacement blocked on capacity, a replacement already backed by capacity, repeated ticks, failed deletion, and a schedule-only tick. Run the Iris unit suite and repository lint/review gates, then verify on a dev controller before enabling the policy on the reserved v4 pool. No live drain or controller restart is part of this triage.

The main risk is evicting work while GCP still cannot create the replacement slice. The ledger and deletion confirmation prevent double-spending chips; the grace period and in-flight check limit repeated churn. Before enabling this for the production pool, confirm that the configured `quota_pool` maps to one fungible GCP reservation and that its physical budget is 1,024 chips.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 **Design for a fix (for review before code).**

## Prior work checked

- **Issue 6217** ("Higher Queues Should Preempt Across Node Types for Reserved Compute", closed as stale on 2026-08-29) asked for the same thing. Its research comment proposed relaxing the scheduler's same-variant gate on reserved capacity and left three questions open:
  1. What is a "reserved pool"?
  2. How do we stay thrash-safe?
  3. Which bands may cross?

  This design answers all three.
- Echo searches on reservation, priority and drain found no other decision. `lib/iris` docs have nothing on this.
- The config already has the pool key: every size of a `tpu_pools` entry gets `quota_pool = "<pool>/<zone>"` (`config.py:1509`), for example `v4-reserved/us-central2-b`. Groups with `capacity_type: reserved` and the same `quota_pool` draw on one reservation.

## Which component acts: the autoscaler, with the controller doing the preemption

Relaxing the scheduler gate alone does not work:
- The preemptor cannot land this tick. A v4-1024 needs a new slice, not freed v4-8 workers.
- The preempted batch tasks go back to PENDING and are re-placed on the freed workers of their own slices on the next tick, because those slices are still READY and their groups still have demand. Nothing is returned to the reservation.

The capacity owner must remove the slices. The autoscaler is the only component that knows all four facts that matter:
- the pool,
- that the preemptor's group has a slice waiting on the cloud and for how long,
- each slice's chip count,
- which slices are READY.

**Change:**
1. **`DemandEntry` gains `priority_band`.** The residual-demand builder in `scheduling/policy.py` already reads the job row.
2. **`WorkerStatus` gains `max_running_band`,** the highest band of the tasks running on that worker (none when idle). The controller already builds `WorkerStatusMap` from running tasks.
3. **New pure function `plan_reservation_reclaim(groups, demand, worker_status, now)`** in a new `autoscaler/reclaim.py`. It returns `ReclaimDecision(preemptor_job, pool, victim_slices, chips_needed, chips_freed)`.
4. **`AutoscaleResult` gains `reclaim: list[ReclaimDecision]`.** The controller folds each decision in one transaction:
   - Mark every task on the victim workers PREEMPTED, with the reason `reservation reclaim for <job> in <pool>`, through the existing preemption transition. This counts against the victim's preemption-retry budget, the same as ordinary preemption.
   - Fence those workers, then call the existing `remove_capacity`. The slices are deleted, so their chips go back to the reservation, and the cloud then fulfils the preemptor's waiting queued resource.

## Trigger (all must hold)

- **Reserved demand:** a coscheduled demand entry of band B is routed to a group with `capacity_type: reserved`.
- **Waiting on the cloud:** that group has a slice that is not READY because it is waiting on the cloud (BOOTING or REQUESTING for the queued resource).
- **Unmet long enough:** that slice has existed for at least `reclaim_min_wait`, default 10 min. A short wait usually means normal provisioning, not a full reservation.
- **No recent reclaim:** no reclaim for this pool within the last `reclaim_cooldown`, default 30 min, unless the earlier reclaimed slice has since become READY. If the cloud still cannot place after a drain (for example, the reservation is also used outside Iris), Iris does not keep killing jobs.

## Victim choice

- **Candidates:** READY slices in other groups (any size) with the same `quota_pool` and `capacity_type: reserved`.
  - Every worker of a candidate is idle or runs only bands strictly lower than B. **Equal or higher bands are never touched.**
  - A slice with even one equal-or-higher task is skipped whole.
- **Order:**
  1. Idle slices first. They cost nothing; scale-down would have taken them after the idle threshold anyway.
  2. Then the lowest band first (batch before interactive).
  3. Then fewest chips first.
  4. Then the youngest slice, so the least work is lost.
- **Stop** as soon as the freed chips reach `chips_needed`, the chip count of the waiting slice.
- **All or nothing:** if the candidates cannot reach `chips_needed`, drain nothing and record `reclaim_blocked` with the shortfall.
- **One preemptor per pool per tick:** the highest band first, then the oldest.

**Limit:** Iris does not know how many chips are free in the reservation; GCP only reports the queued resource as waiting. So `chips_needed` assumes none are free. That may drain somewhat more than strictly needed, never less. A follow-up could add an optional per-pool `reserved_chips` budget to the config and subtract live usage.

## Recording

- Every reclaim is written to the autoscaler action log (`_log_action("reservation_reclaim", ...)`), as scale-ups and scale-downs are today. The entry carries:
  - the preemptor job and its band,
  - the pool,
  - each victim slice with its chips and its jobs' bands,
  - `chips_needed` and `chips_freed`.
- `reclaim_blocked` is recorded the same way.
- Victim tasks get the preemption reason above, so `iris job` views show why they stopped.

## Tests (existing fakes; no cluster)

All pure-function tests of `plan_reservation_reclaim`, plus one controller fold test:
1. Today's case: a reserved pool full of batch v4-8, v4-32, v4-64, v4-128, v4-256 and v4-512 slices, and a production v4-1024 waiting past `reclaim_min_wait`.
   - Expect idle slices, then the smallest batch slices, until 512 chips are freed.
   - Expect no interactive slice to be drained while batch slices suffice.
2. Equal-band victims are never chosen, and a slice with one equal-band task is skipped whole.
3. Below `reclaim_min_wait`, or inside the cooldown: no reclaim.
4. Not enough lower-band chips: no drain, and `reclaim_blocked` is recorded.
5. A preemptible or on-demand pool, or a different `quota_pool`: never reclaimed from.
6. Controller fold:
   - victim tasks go to PREEMPTED with the reason, and their workers are fenced and passed to `remove_capacity`;
   - the victim jobs' preemption-retry counts go up by one;
   - the preemptor is not placed in the same tick.

## Not in scope

- Solo (non-coscheduled) preemptors.
- Preemptible pools, where freeing chips gives no guarantee.
- Any change to deployment or a live cluster.

The settings live in the autoscaler config: `reservation_reclaim.enabled` (proposed default: on), `min_wait` (10 min) and `cooldown` (30 min). Operators can tune reclaim, or turn it off, per cluster.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 Draft fix: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11617. It follows the design above, with two changes:
- **Off by default:** reclaim runs only for pools listed in `defaults.autoscaler.reservation_reclaim.quota_pools`.
- **Tasks fail through the worker-failure path:** a victim's tasks become `WORKER_FAILED` on their preemption budget, through the existing `_remove_worker_capacity` path, not `PREEMPTED`.

The PR lists the two choices left to the Iris owners (default off, and which bands may be victims) and the limits.
