spillover_issues.author: penfever
spillover_issues.body:
`grade_math_candidate` converts math_verify's `TimeoutException` into `GradingInfraError("math verifier deadline exhausted")`. For some tasks the timeout is deterministic: every attempt of the same task parses a candidate/reference combination that exceeds the deadline, so the task records only infrastructure attempts and the source stays permanently pending — retries cannot change the outcome.

Observed in small-v16 (`2026.11.14.43/small-v16`, exited successfully), source `pafitis:hardmath` (13 of its 100 selected tasks are pending):
- 78 infrastructure attempts across 13 tasks; the sampled receipts show 11 distinct tasks whose every attempt ended with `GradeResult(status=Outcome.INFRA_ERROR, error='math verifier deadline exhausted')`, e.g. `hardmath-1e2483b884b23134518281560e7093cdb0689ff00aaf5ef6de464e5ff9aef213`, `hardmath-0a3338878b6532ef6fae4cbde3092f9653bf84206b34288958ef7c77044040bf`, `hardmath-986bc6ec98013391ee11cc99227c50a728625b18521826dbbd5cc41a845d73c8`.
- Every attempt consumed a full solver trial (model inference + judge) before the deadline failure.

Reproduce:
1. Grade a `pafitis:hardmath` candidate listed above against its TaskSpec reference with the protocol's math-verify profile and deadline.
2. `math_verify` raises `TimeoutException` inside its parse/verify; the grader maps it to `GradingInfraError`; the trial records `INFRA_ERROR` with no reward.
3. Repeating the attempt reproduces the same timeout.

Expected: a deterministic per-task deadline failure should be distinguishable from transient infrastructure load — e.g. a larger or shape-specific parse deadline, a cheaper pre-check for pathological candidate/reference pairs, or a typed condition that stops retrying and reports the task as ungradeable instead of consuming the full attempt budget.

Grader code: `lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/modes/grade_math.py:316-318` (`except TimeoutException ... raise GradingInfraError("math verifier deadline exhausted")`), deadline via `math_verify.utils.timeout` at `lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/modes/grade_math.py:325`.

Evidence receipts (S3, no PII): `s3://marin-rno2a/marin/rl-data/atlas/difficulty/2026.11.14.43/small-v16/trials/<sha256("pafitis:hardmath")>/attempts/<task_key>/*/attempt.json`.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

Verifyit maps every math-verify deadline during reference parsing, candidate parsing, or comparison to the same infrastructure error. In draft PR #11277, Atlas runs another full trial after an unscored attempt and resumes every task without a scored result, so repeated verifier deadlines consume solver work and leave the source pending. The receipts establish repeated failures, but do not yet show which grading phase timed out or whether the candidate text was the same across attempts.

**Relevant code**

- [`grade_math.py#L309-L318`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/0169e8a4feccf4db58a3b3fac50c5f24c78be473/lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/modes/grade_math.py#L309-L318) — collapses deadline phases
- [`grade_math.py#L48-L54`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/0169e8a4feccf4db58a3b3fac50c5f24c78be473/lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/modes/grade_math.py#L48-L54) — five-second main-thread deadline
- [`difficulty_trials.py#L370-L387`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7c86252b6c790c1d9feb1fc02ceb025359fe8303/experiments/post_training/task_curation/difficulty_trials.py#L370-L387) — retries unscored trials
- [`difficulty_trials.py#L494-L508`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7c86252b6c790c1d9feb1fc02ceb025359fe8303/experiments/post_training/task_curation/difficulty_trials.py#L494-L508) — resumes unscored tasks
- [`difficulty.py#L275-L315`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7c86252b6c790c1d9feb1fc02ceb025359fe8303/lib/finestore/src/finestore/rl/difficulty.py#L275-L315) — excludes failures from scored coverage

# Proposed Fix

1. Replay several affected TaskSpecs and archived candidate outputs in the pinned grader environment. Record the reference, candidate, profile, and input hashes, and identify whether each timeout occurs in reference parsing, candidate parsing, or comparison. Test the same input again under the same deadline before treating it as deterministic.
2. Carry a typed timeout phase through Verifyit's infrastructure verdict. Run a bounded reference preflight before solver inference in the grader's main process or an isolated child process; the current signal deadline is disabled in worker threads. A confirmed fixed-reference timeout becomes a terminal, unscored task condition. Candidate-dependent timeouts remain infrastructure failures while retryable; after a cumulative retry cap, record a terminal `grader_blocked` reason without assigning a zero reward.
3. Extend Atlas's attempt receipts and recovery filter with a terminal blocked status and reason. Add `blocked_tasks` to measurement accounting, so `scored + retryable pending + blocked` equals the selected population; use a distinct blocked source status when no retryable tasks remain. Historical infrastructure receipts remain unclassified. Blocked tasks never enter `n` or `solved`. Coordinate the Atlas portion with draft PR #11277, which owns these paths.

Test the fixed-reference path before any solver call, candidate/compare timeout classification, recovery across campaign versions, and unchanged scoring for gradeable tasks. Replaying the sampled HARDMath tasks should show no repeated full trials after a terminal diagnosis and no invented solver scores. A longer verifier deadline should be evaluated from the replay timings before changing the global five-second limit.

comments.author: XiaoyuanWang111
comments.body:
🤖 I replayed the `math` mode on the pinned HARDMath mirror to see which step runs out and whether it depends on the reply. The comparison runs out, and only for some replies: the conversion check and a reply equal to the reference finish on every row, while a reply that is another equation often reaches the deadline.

The data is `pafitis/HARDMath_processed_training` at 937e9f10, all 702 rows. Each contract is built from `ground_truths` as `math_answer_task` builds it and graded through `verifyit.grade.run` on main, one process per call. 684 rows convert; the other 18 have the unparseable reference of #11510. The replies are constructed. I have no access to the stored attempts, so I cannot say which replies the 13 pending tasks received.

| reply | scored 1 | scored 0 | deadline |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| no answer file (the conversion check) | 0 | 684 | 0 |
| `\boxed{reference}` | 684 | 0 | 0 |
| `\boxed{42}` | 0 | 684 | 0 |
| `\boxed{reference of the next row of the same question type}` | 0 | 491 | 193 |
| `\boxed{reference with its first number raised by 1}` | 0 | 532 | 152 |

- **Which rows.** The 193 are 102 of the 125 ODE rows and 91 of the 101 symbolic nondimensionalization rows. Their references are equations, `[y = …, y = …]` and `\epsilon=…`. The other three question types (458 rows) never reach the deadline.
- **Which step.** In all 193 calls, parsing the reference and parsing the reply return within 0.5 s. The time goes into math-verify's comparison of the two equations (`sympy_compare_relational`): its symbolic equality check, then solving both equations with SymPy (`sympy_solve_and_compare`). With the deadline set to 20 s, 41 of the 193 comparisons finish, in 5.1 to 19.6 s, and 152 do not.
- **Which replies.** For symbolic nondimensionalization, the reference with one exponent changed reaches the deadline on 81 of 89 rows. The reference regrouped as `\epsilon=\frac{a_{1} a_{3}^{p/q}}{a_{2}^{p/q} a_{3}}` (`p/q` is its exponent), which is equal for positive coefficients, reaches it on 74 of 89 and scores 0 on the other 15. The right-hand side alone, without `\epsilon=`, scores 1.0 on all 101.

For the retry limit of #11518 this means the verdict follows the reply. A task is blocked once three consecutive attempts reach the deadline, which here means three replies that are another equation, wrong or regrouped; a reply in the reference's own form scores 1.0 in under a second. The blocked tasks leave `n`, and the tasks the solver got right stay.

One case, row 9 of the train split, with row 20's answer (the same expression with exponent 17/6) as the wrong reply:

```python
from verifyit.grade import GradingInfraError
from verifyit.modes.grade_math import grade_math_candidate
from verifyit.spec import MathSpec, MathType

reference = r"\epsilon=\frac{a_{1} \left(\frac{a_{3}}{a_{2}}\right)^{\frac{19}{9}}}{a_{3}}"
spec = MathSpec(expected=reference, math_type=MathType.EQUATION)
for reply in (reference, "42", reference.replace("19}{9", "17}{6")):
    try:
        print(grade_math_candidate(spec, reply).reward, reply)
    except GradingInfraError as error:
        print(error, reply)
```

It prints `1.0`, `0.0` and `math verifier deadline exhausted`.

On the conversion side, `convert_hardmath` passes `ground_truths` whole, so the reference keeps its left-hand side. The two older HARDMath loaders (`_prepare_hardmath`, `_hardmath_records`) keep only the right-hand side and reject answers that contain `[`. With those two rules 383 rows remain, and with the next row's answer as the reply none of them reaches the deadline; the slowest call takes 0.49 s.

spillover_issues.author: XiaoyuanWang111
spillover_issues.body:
508 of the 1,000 `time_intervals` rows of the generated Reasoning Gym source grade only on the day they were generated. On a later day [the grade script](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d83e7766c5a5b9bec43cdd26eccc71a54dcf9bfd/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/reasoning_gym/reasoning_gym_grade.py#L55-L57) exits 1 with `ValueError: Regenerated entry differs from the recorded entry` for every reply, the row's own answer included, and [grading](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d83e7766c5a5b9bec43cdd26eccc71a54dcf9bfd/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/runtime/grading.py#L350-L353) records an infrastructure error. [Training](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d83e7766c5a5b9bec43cdd26eccc71a54dcf9bfd/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/task_projections.py#L191-L209) then leaves the rollout out of the loss. `snowball-100k` draws 20,800 rows of this source; I did not count its `time_intervals` rows.

Reproduce:

1. From the repository root, run:

   ```bash
   PYTHONHASHSEED=0 uv run --package marin-verifyit --extra reasoning-gym python - <<'EOF'
   import sys

   sys.path.insert(0, "experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/reasoning_gym")
   import generate
   import reasoning_gym

   task = "time_intervals"
   data = reasoning_gym.create_dataset(task, size=generate.ROWS_PER_TASK, seed=generate.task_seed(task))
   entry = generate.encoded(data[2])
   print(entry["question"])
   print(entry["metadata"]["start_time"], "|", entry["metadata"]["end_time"])
   time_only = ("time", "time_seconds", "time_ms")
   print(sum(data[index]["metadata"]["task_type"] in time_only for index in range(generate.ROWS_PER_TASK)))
   EOF
   ```

2. The first line is a question with times only: `A meeting started at 01:01:14 and ended at 06:10:42. How long was the meeting? Answer in HH:MM:SS.` The second line is the entry's `metadata.start_time` and `metadata.end_time`. They carry the date of the run, for example `2026-11-16 01:01:14 | 2026-11-16 06:10:42`. The third line is `508`, the number of entries of the task types `time`, `time_seconds` and `time_ms`.
3. The row's contract stores the entry as encoded on the generation day, so on a later day the comparison at L56 fails for these entries.

Expected: a row's own answer scores 1.0 on any day.

`reasoning-gym` 0.1.25 parses the time-only strings with `dateutil.parser.parse` (`reasoning_gym/arithmetic/time_intervals.py` L104-L105), and `dateutil` fills a missing date with the current day in the process's local time. The question and the answer are the same on every day. [The converter](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d83e7766c5a5b9bec43cdd26eccc71a54dcf9bfd/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/reasoning_gym/tasks.py#L261-L262) rejects an entry whose `reproducible` flag is false, but [the generator](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d83e7766c5a5b9bec43cdd26eccc71a54dcf9bfd/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/reasoning_gym/generate.py#L141-L150) sets that flag by regenerating the entry in the same process, so it is true for these rows.

I did not grade a stored row. I encoded the 1,000 entries with `datetime.now()` fixed to 2026-11-04 inside `dateutil`'s parser and ran the grade script on 2026-11-16: 508 regenerated entries differ from the recorded ones, entry 2 exits 1 on its own answer, and entry 0 (task type `datetime`) prints 1.0. Among the first 200 entries of each of the 104 generated tasks, regenerated on another day and in two other time zones, no other task has entries that pass the `reproducible` flag and differ.

spillover_issues.author: XiaoyuanWang111
spillover_issues.body:
After #11516, the scorers of six generated Reasoning Gym tasks still raise on a malformed reply. The [generated](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d83e7766c5a5b9bec43cdd26eccc71a54dcf9bfd/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/reasoning_gym/reasoning_gym_grade.py#L58) and [Nemotron Ultra](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d83e7766c5a5b9bec43cdd26eccc71a54dcf9bfd/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/nemotron_ultra/reasoning_gym_grade.py#L42-L46) grade scripts then exit 1, and [grading](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d83e7766c5a5b9bec43cdd26eccc71a54dcf9bfd/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/runtime/grading.py#L350-L353) records an infrastructure error. The verifyit `reasoning-gym` mode [re-raises](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d83e7766c5a5b9bec43cdd26eccc71a54dcf9bfd/lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/modes/grade_reasoning_gym.py#L115-L120) and writes an `infra_error` verdict. [Training](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d83e7766c5a5b9bec43cdd26eccc71a54dcf9bfd/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/task_projections.py#L191-L209) leaves a rollout with an infrastructure error out of the loss, so such a reply costs the model nothing. #11516 scores such a reply 0.0 for `prime_factorization` only.

| task | reply | exception | entries that raise, of the first 30 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `boxnet` | `0` | `TypeError` | 30 |
| `game_of_life` | `{}` | `KeyError` | 30 |
| `coin_flip` | `1e400` | `OverflowError` | 30 |
| `propositional_logic` | 5,000 `(` then 5,000 `)` | `RecursionError` | 30 |
| `calendar_arithmetic` | 400 digits `9` | `OverflowError` | 12 |
| `time_intervals` | 400 digits `9` | `OverflowError` | 7 |

Reproduce:

1. From the repository root, run:

   ```bash
   PYTHONHASHSEED=0 uv run --package marin-verifyit --extra reasoning-gym python - <<'EOF'
   import sys

   sys.path.insert(0, "experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/reasoning_gym")
   import generate
   import reasoning_gym

   REPLIES = {
       "boxnet": "0",
       "game_of_life": "{}",
       "coin_flip": "1e400",
       "propositional_logic": "(" * 5000 + ")" * 5000,
       "calendar_arithmetic": "9" * 400,
       "time_intervals": "9" * 400,
   }
   for task, reply in REPLIES.items():
       data = reasoning_gym.create_dataset(task, size=generate.ROWS_PER_TASK, seed=generate.task_seed(task))
       score = reasoning_gym.get_score_answer_fn(task)
       raised = []
       for index in range(30):
           try:
               score(reply, data[index])
           except Exception as error:
               raised.append(type(error).__name__)
       print(task, len(raised), sorted(set(raised)))
   EOF
   ```

2. Each line prints a task, the number of its first 30 entries on which the scorer raises, and the exception type, as in the table.

Expected: a reply that a scorer cannot parse scores 0.0.

`boxnet` raises on any reply that is a JSON number. The generated script reads the text after the last `Answer:`, so the reply `Answer: 42` raises there too. I ran 87 fixed replies on the first 30 entries of each of the 104 generated tasks: no other task raises, and the six raise on all three grading paths when each path scores the generated entries.

Three of the six are in the Nemotron blend's part of the released validation panel (`open-athena/Snowball-Smartie-RL-2026.10.15.32-Data`). With the panel's own grade script, the same replies raise on all four of its `game_of_life` tasks, all seven of its `propositional_logic` tasks and one of its four `calendar_arithmetic` tasks.

spillover_issues.author: XiaoyuanWang111
spillover_issues.body:
Four generated Reasoning Gym tasks give full reward to a reply that does not depend on the question. `reasoning_gym_generated` holds 1,000 rows of each.

- `game_of_life_halting`: every non-blank reply scores 1.0 on all 1,000 entries. The scorer compares `bool(reply)` with `bool(answer)`, and every answer is the string `True` or `False`. [The generator](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d83e7766c5a5b9bec43cdd26eccc71a54dcf9bfd/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/reasoning_gym/generate.py#L77-L86) records the reward of the fixed wrong answer `definitely wrong` for every row. For these 1,000 rows the recorded reward is 1.0, and [`convert_generated`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d83e7766c5a5b9bec43cdd26eccc71a54dcf9bfd/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/reasoning_gym/tasks.py#L256-L271) stores the record without reading it.
- `complex_arithmetic`: the reply `NaN` scores 1.0 on all 1,000 entries. The scorer returns `min(1.0, math.exp(-distance))`, which is 1.0 when the distance is NaN.
- `coin_flip`: the reply `0` scores 1.0 on 939 of the 1,000 entries. The scorer of `reasoning-gym` 0.1.25 gives partial reward for a matching prefix and divides by the length of the shorter string, so the one-character reply `0` matches every answer that starts with `0.`.
- `propositional_logic`: the reply `P ∨ Q` scores 1.0 on 820 of the 1,000 entries. The scorer accepts any conclusion that follows from the premises, and a disjunction that names a premise follows from it.

Reproduce:

1. From the repository root, run:

   ```bash
   PYTHONHASHSEED=0 uv run --package marin-verifyit --extra reasoning-gym python - <<'EOF'
   import sys

   sys.path.insert(0, "experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/reasoning_gym")
   import generate
   import reasoning_gym

   replies = (
       ("game_of_life_halting", "x"),
       ("complex_arithmetic", "NaN"),
       ("coin_flip", "0"),
       ("propositional_logic", "P ∨ Q"),
   )
   for task, reply in replies:
       data = reasoning_gym.create_dataset(task, size=generate.ROWS_PER_TASK, seed=generate.task_seed(task))
       score = reasoning_gym.get_score_answer_fn(task)
       print(task, repr(reply), sum(score(reply, data[index]) == 1.0 for index in range(generate.ROWS_PER_TASK)))
   EOF
   ```

2. It prints `game_of_life_halting 'x' 1000`, `complex_arithmetic 'NaN' 1000`, `coin_flip '0' 939` and `propositional_logic 'P ∨ Q' 820`.

Expected: a constant reply does not earn full reward.

The recorded wrong answer scores 0 on `complex_arithmetic` and `coin_flip` and 0.05 or 0.25 on `propositional_logic`, so that record shows only the first of the four. Two of the four are in the Nemotron blend's part of the released validation panel (`open-athena/Snowball-Smartie-RL-2026.10.15.32-Data`): with the panel's own grade script, `P ∨ Q` scores 1.0 on six of its seven `propositional_logic` tasks and `NaN` on its one `complex_arithmetic` task.

I tried 44 constant replies on the first 100 entries of every generated task. No fifth task gives the full reward on more than a quarter of the entries to a constant that is not the entry's answer.

spillover_issues.author: karansag
spillover_issues.body:
## Summary

With CUDA module loading set to LAZY and XLA autotune level 0, the observed 64-H100 Long Loop runs showed slow steps or stalled on the first stock executable call. With EAGER at autotune level 0, the first stock call completed in four of four runs: carried-state v9 (78.8 s), C-replay r3 (56.1 s), C-e12 (74.4 s), and fresh-state H without a round trip (58.2 s). Fresh H's second call took 49.1 s and its first loss was 0.6393635273, matching the other fresh H runs that completed after a round trip.

The comparison leaves the runtime mechanism open. An older EAGER run with autotune level 4 on a different graph stalled in `cuModuleLoadData`. See [the carried-state comparison](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11646#issuecomment-6970458310) and [the draft launch change](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11647).

## Symptom

The Long Loop Grug MoE SFT loop can stall in its first compiled train step on eight hosts with eight H100s each. All 64 GPUs stayed busy, but the step did not complete. Among the Long Loop runs examined, the stall has been observed only in graphs with expert weights in MuonH. The stalled loop is on the Long Loop branch, not main. A related first-update stall on a different layout is tracked in [the Snowball optimizer issue](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11440); a common cause is not established.

## Observed setup and expected behavior

Run the Long Loop SFT graph from commit `917055e33f44ddb3b5e1a927eab0793e7a9f4501` with replica=1, data=8, expert=1 and context=8 across eight H100 hosts, with expert matrices in MuonH. The first train step should finish and subsequent steps should run without a host round trip. Two runs stalled before completing that step.

The successful reconstruction-only diagnostic snapshots the entire train state to host memory, deletes its device arrays, and restores the state before the first call. Its first three steps took 80.7, 49.0 and 41.1 seconds. In a separate paired diagnostic, a direct compiled call and the subsequent stock call took 52.5 and 46.1 seconds; the latter followed a direct execution and a host state reconstruction.

## Evidence and limits

Isolated expert momentum, projection and Newton–Schulz probes completed. In the paired diagnostic, StableHLO and optimized HLO were byte-identical and all 76 input leaf metadata entries matched; the stock call made no rank-zero compiler requests. Disabling the persistent executable cache did not prevent the stall, and the successful reconstruction run used autotune level zero. Its pre-reconstruction buffer inventory found no shared buffer start addresses and no pending shards on all 64 ranks. The cancelled stalled attempts did not retain those buffer inventories, so this does not establish their buffer state.

The cause is unknown. Whether the same mechanism also explains the earlier arm's 115–132 second steady steps remains open. The highest observed per-task sample was 146.2 GiB against a 640 GiB allocation. The snapshot peak was not measured.

The v7a2 rank-zero runtime inventory reports JAX, jaxlib, jax-cuda13-plugin and jax-cuda13-pjrt 0.11.1 and CUDA runtime 13.0.96. The source declares `jax[cuda13]==0.11.0` in its root dependency set; the installed rank-zero inventory is the runtime observation. All eight task image pull events identify `ghcr.io/marin-community/iris-task@sha256:b5b474d80ca79f996049cc0cf700ab93ab2d41a4d9b8a91afc43ce11bf44d974`.

Evidence is stored in 02a temporary prefixes and expires after 30 days:

- Reconstruction run: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/long-loop-436/e12/h-muon-prelude-v7a2-20261118/fresh/` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Flong-loop-436%2Fe12%2Fh-muon-prelude-v7a2-20261118%2Ffresh%2F)).
- Paired HLO evidence: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/long-loop-436/e12/h-muon-dispatch-v6-20261118/fresh/evidence/` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Flong-loop-436%2Fe12%2Fh-muon-dispatch-v6-20261118%2Ffresh%2Fevidence%2F)).

# Research

The published Long Loop `train_step` compiles gradient accumulation and `optimizer.update` into one donated-state call, so the stalled step does not identify the blocked operation. The successful host-state reconstruction and direct-call diagnostic narrow the conditions but do not establish a buffer aliasing cause; the cancelled stalls have no buffer inventories. The cited source commit `917055e` is not available in the repository, and open PRs #11639 and #11640 change expert MuonH grouping and configuration while explicitly leaving this stall unresolved.

**Relevant code**
- [`train.py#L1037-L1077`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/c6676c91efe773f251d455f97c59e060b49faf1b/experiments/post_training/long_loop/sft_runtime/train.py#L1037-L1077) — gradients and optimizer share one JIT call.
- [`optimizer.py#L96-L123`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/grug/moe/optimizer.py#L96-L123) — generic MuonH update path.
- [PR #11639](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11639) — stacked-expert backend and grouping change.
- [Issue #11440](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11440) — related XLA stall; common cause unproven.

# Proposed Fix

1. Preserve the exact `917055e` diagnostic source, launch configuration, runtime inventory, first-step input metadata, and compact HLO artifacts before the 30-day evidence prefixes expire. Pin the image and the optimizer mask used by each run; the public prototype branch is not an exact reproduction of that commit.
2. Run bounded, fresh 64-GPU repeats of the direct first call and host-state reconstruction from the same initialized state and batch. On each stall, collect all-rank host stacks, two time-separated NCCL RAS counter snapshots, GPU process state, and pre-call buffer inventories. Compare those with completed attempts; current inventories cover only a successful run.
3. With the same state and sharding, place explicit completion boundaries after gradient computation and after the MuonH update. Compare expert-MuonH and expert-Adam controls, then reduce the blocked phase to a smaller JAX/PJRT replay if it persists. Treat split-step success as a diagnostic because splitting changes the compiled graph.
4. Patch only the isolated cause. Qualify the result with repeated 64-GPU first steps, at least three finite updates per run, unchanged optimizer numerics, and no host-state reconstruction before or between steps. Keep #11639/#11640 separate unless a matched control implicates their changes.

🤖 **Marin Belay intake: post research ideas for [Marin Belay](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/) here.**

Marin Belay is a human-guided, agent-executed experiment loop that hill-climbs the grug `fast_track` scaling ladder (Paloma macro loss).

**Start with the [contributor guide](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/marin_belay_v1_recipe/experiments/belay/CONTRIBUTING.md)**: how to check an idea against the recipe, pick a Track, follow its runs, and take it up the ladder.

1. **Post one idea per comment**, with a paper link or a short rationale. Add a `Track:` line to pick the baseline; the default is `speedrun` (the 8-minute d512 run). The Belay page lists the Tracks.
2. **A maintainer reviews it** on the Belay admin page and approves it for an agent session, or declines it with a reason.
3. **👀 on your comment means it has been reviewed.** Nothing else is posted here. Plans, results and decline reasons are on the Status page.

**The usual path for an idea:** optionally a `vanilla-*` Track first, for a radical idea or a stronger signal; then `speedrun`, for fast iteration and to check it fits the current recipe; then `hero-mfu` if it will change MFU a lot; then `ladder`. Maintainers promote ideas into the recipe from those results.

**Tracks** (the `Track:` line):

| Track | Runs against | Hardware |
|---|---|---|
| `speedrun` (default) | The 8-minute d512 run of the current recipe; judged at equal data, then equal time if the step time changes | 1× 8×H100 |
| `competitive-d512` … `competitive-d1280` | The current recipe at one ladder rung, compared with its finished baseline run | 8×H100; d1280 on 4 nodes |
| `ladder` | All four `competitive-*` rungs at once, at the baseline's step count. After a `hero-mfu` result, each rung's steps are adjusted for the MFU change (better MFU, more steps). Without one, the verdict is provisional: the idea needs a `hero-mfu` result before it joins the recipe | as above |
| `moe-d512` … `moe-d1280` | A basic MoE at that rung | 8×H100 |
| `vanilla-d512` … `vanilla-d1280` | A dense baseline at that rung | 8×H100 |
| `hero-mfu` | Step time of the hero GB200 stack; a maintainer runs it | 1 GB200 rack |
| `custom` | A study: runs on other Tracks, then an analysis report with no win/loss verdict; needs a node and hours budget | per study |

Wins are judged on Paloma macro loss with a noise band of 0.005 (`hero-mfu`: step time, ±0.5%).

**Example comments**

> Try warming the MuonH momentum up from 0.85 to 0.98 over the first 10% of training, as modded-nanogpt does.

> Track: moe-d768
> Replace the router's sigmoid combine weights with softmax over the top-8 experts.

> Track: ladder
> Take X0221 (CPLM Plus) up the ladder with the settings of its speedrun win.

> Track: custom
> Measure how the stable rank of each attention projection changes over a full d512 run, from checkpoints every 1,000 steps.

**The Belay app** ([public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-…](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/)):

- **[Belay](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/):** the project. It covers the current recipe, the scaling ladder and its projection, the timeline, the gates an idea passes, the Tracks, the data and the starter kit.
- **[Status](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/#status):** every idea and its results across the gates (Dense, speedrun, Hero MFU, projection, recipe), live runs and queue, and the agent log with one thread per idea (`#status/X####`).
- **[Hero MFU](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/#mfu):** hero-scale throughput, with each MFU change on the GB200 stack and its branch.
- **[Admin](https://applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/#admin)** (maintainers, signed in to Marina): review and approve or decline ideas, with instructions and node, hours and priority grants. It also sets the node cap, dispatch and GitHub reactions.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
In latentMoE, we can try initializing the up/down projections as semi-orthogonal matrices and either:

A: using an orthogonality-preserving optimizer such as the one introduced in https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06218 to update them
or
B: freezing them, keeping them semi-orthogonal and not updating them at all, while relying the rest of the NN to adapt

Rationale: up/down projections in latentMoE are themselves small, shared by all experts of the same layer, therefore not really having the capability to do meaningful computation for the whole NN. We should see them as information-preserving maps instead, and worry more about gradient pathology/distortion, rather than the potential loss of the degree of freedom/expressivity by using semi-orthogonal matrices.
Also if we take the "no meaningful computation" hypothesis really seriously, option B should only have negligible performance degradation compared to A. And if we use B, no new optimizer and no new hyperparameter tuning are needed.

comments.body:
Tune muonh lr and nesterov momentum for q/k projections separately from the rest of the matrix parameters.

Rationale: I always thought tuning the optimizer hyperparameters of all different components of a neural network, although mundane, is the right thing to do. Falcon H1's way of doing things (Table 8 in https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.22448) is closer to what we should do if we have enough tuning budget.

But if we don't want to risk wasting a lot of experiments on possibly nonexistent gains, we should rely on our intuitions on which components might benefit the most from a separate set of hyperparameters in order to narrow the targets, and my best guesses are q/k projections. They historically caused trouble by being much less tolerant to high lr, and people had to invent qk norm to help with that. However, after qk norm was introduced, now we don't know which one is true:

1. qk norm is a partial alleviation, and q/k projections should still be optimized with a more conservative setting
2. qk norm stabilizes things so much that it opens the opportunity for q/k projections to be optimized with a more aggressively setting

And we may find out by tuning their optimizer setting separately.

The suggestion above is based on the GQA/MQA arch with qk norm. For MLA, the naive first guess about which parameters should be optimized with a separate set of hyperparameters is W_q, W_dkv and W_uk, though excluding W_dkv or including W_uv seems to be equally convincing.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Attention residuals q embedding:
In addition to a data independent q vector for each layer, we also use a per-layer embedding q_e, similar to the value embedding, and add it to q before computing the dot product with k, so the attention residual formula before normalization turns from

exp(q^T RMSNorm(k))

into

exp((q + q_e(token_index))^T RMSNorm(k))

q_e should be initialized as all 0.

Rationale: In the attention residuals paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15031), the authors ablated input dependent q in Table 4, and showed that it could further decrease loss, but excluded it from the default implementation because of extra compute and overhead. The "token dependent q" in this proposal is a compromise between cheap "data independent q" and expensive "q calculated from internal states using a dxd projection".

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Reconsider per-element attention gate, and either variant seems viable.

1. a linear projection with the same shape of the W_v projection, followed by sigmoid, like how Kimi K3 does it.
2. a down projection to a smaller vector, followed by a Swish nonlinearity, an up projection, then sigmoid, like how the current GatedNorm does it.

Rationale: the current Marin recipe has reduced the total number of MLA layers, by using a KDA+MLA hybrid, therefore the extra overhead of per-element gates compared to per-head ones becomes smaller.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Log and analyze some of these statistics during training (if some of these are too expensive then do it every tens or hundreds of steps):

1. Stable rank of each projection-like parameter matrix. If it gets very low over time, the frobenius norm which muonh controls no longer serves as a good proxy of spectral norm, and it may be a pathology case when scaling up.
2. Max row norm vs mean row norm of each projection-like parameter matrix. Unusually large row norm is a cause of large (element-wise)activations.
3. RMSNorm gains that become very far away from the initial 1.
4. Max element vs element rms of each layer's output.

Rationale: these indicators may provide some information to help us in both ways:

1. If we decide some of the anomalies are undesirable, we can come up with mitigations, and if the anomalies are local to some of the layers, mitigations can be local too.
2. If we decide some of the anomalies are desirable, we can try inducing the desired effects via explicit ways and prevent the side effects of the implicit behavior, like how the GatedNorm paper discovered that activation outliers are implicitly used for scaling down other activations, and came up with explicit gating to do that instead.

These are just a few indicators I can think of right now, and there has to be much more. When we have other aspects of the model we are interested with, we can add them to the list.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Add an extra loss term to counter the indefinite stretching effect to s, or normalize s and y in the original aux term, in the experiments of Batch 178 (MLP compression).

Choice 1: Instead of lambda * ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) we should use lambda * ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) + lambda_1 * ||s||^n
where n can be 2 or (4 and higher) depending on whether we want the counter force to be smoother or more "hard cap like".

Choice 2: let s' = s / ||s|| and y' = y / ||y||, and the aux term should become lambda * ||s' - sg(y')||^2
where y = s + r

Rationale: in the aux loss in batch 178, under the random vector assumption, s and r are approximately orthogonal because they are high dimensional, therefore by pythagorean theorem ||s + r||^2 has a very high probability of being larger than ||s||^2, no matter what training phase we are at. In order for the aux loss to minimize ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) it would both rotate s to be more aligned to (s + r) and stretch s longer to match the norm of (s + r). This optimization pressure of raw norm stretching would never stop at any phase of training. This seems to be the opposite of what we want for a regularized neural network, and might be the real reason why Batch 178 didn't show improvements.

Of course now in choice 1, lambda_1 also needs tuning and my intuition is to start with a value smaller than lambda.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Try warmup of muonh nesterov momentum, and see if it could shift the optimal momentum from 0.95 to higher ones.

Like how modded-nanogpt introduced it since record 9, start with a lower momentum like 0.85, and linearly increase it to the value we want over the warmup period. Spend more steps in the momentum warmup (like 10% or 20% of total) than common lr warmup settings (<5%). Try higher final momentum such as 0.98 and see whether the momentum warmup schedule could make them better than the default 0.95.

Rationale: 0.95 is a safe number that's widely used, and the kimi paper reported that tuning it makes minimal difference. However, the lack of success from a a higher momentum may be caused by the early-late training dynamic discrepancy, and if this problem is alleviated, it might have some extra potential after training reaches the stabilized phase. A momentum warmup can help with the discrepancy by forgetting gradient information quicker in the early phase. The ademamix optimizer paper has some empirical evidence that the momentum warmup period should be sufficiently long. Since the update size is at the same scale after the short lr warmup finishes, long momentum warmup doesn't have the problem of "too little accumulated update" so it wouldn't require retuning lr and its schedule.

comments.author: bethehand
comments.body:
**Report the Paloma macro without `ptb` and `wikitext_103` next to the macro, and prefer it for calls near the bar.**

I paired each d512 Belay run (`lc1-*` in `marin_moe`) with its `-s1` twin, which has the same config apart from `trainer.seed`: 404 pairs from Sept 25 to Oct 8. These numbers are for the 305 configs near the frontier, i.e. within 0.01 of their batch median.

- **`ptb` is 1/16 of the macro but carries about a third of its seed noise** (35%). With `wikitext_103` the two carry 42%, by a covariance split.
- **Dropping the two cuts the noise much more than the signal.** Averaging the other 14 subsets cuts the noise SD of a paired Δ by 20%, while real differences between configs shrink by 3%. Signal-to-noise rises 1.4–1.5× (main estimate 1.48×, 95% CI 1.2–1.8), about what 1.5× as many seeds would buy.
- **`ptb`'s differences between configs barely reproduce across seeds:**

| Metric | Seed-to-seed correlation | Noise SD of a 2-seed paired Δ |
|---|---|---|
| Paloma macro, 16 subsets | 0.81 | 0.0016 |
| Without `ptb`, `wikitext_103` | 0.86 | 0.0013 |
| Uncheatable macro | 0.87 | 0.0014 |
| `ptb` alone | 0.10 | 0.013 |

The 0.0016 fits your "two-seed noise of ±0.004" (about 2.5 SD).

**This keeps the objective.** Near the bar, the 14-subset Δ estimates the full macro's true Δ better than the measured macro Δ does: the two-seed RMSE is 0.0009 vs 0.0011. For large changes the two can diverge, so the full macro stays the reference there.

**Two fixed-time calls** (seed 0 / seed 1):

| Call | Macro | Without the two | Uncheatable | `ptb` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Batch 174: candidate 11 vs 10 (same math, 3.5% faster) | −0.0058 / −0.0047 | −0.0075 / −0.0067 | −0.0072 / −0.0070 | +0.013 / +0.029 |
| Batch 200: candidate 12 vs 11 | −0.0001 / −0.0000 | +0.0017 / +0.0045 | +0.0043 / +0.0063 | −0.020 / −0.055 |

- In batch 174, `ptb` hid about a quarter of the gain.
- In batch 200, the exact tie was a fixed-time loss on the other 14 subsets and on Uncheatable. Its two sides ran on different clusters, but candidate 11's equal-step runs on the two clusters agree within 0.002 on these metrics.

**Why these two subsets.** They are the subsets with copies in the hero's training data (#9874), and I picked them before looking at Belay. Choosing subsets by their noise would be fitting the metric. Uncheatable works about as well.

**The bar.** You can keep 0.005 on the 14-subset Δ, for fewer false wins. Or you can lower it to about 0.004, which keeps today's false-win rate; with the observed tails the matching value is 0.0042.

Method, code and per-run numbers: https://github.com/bethehand/marin-hero-forecast/tree/main/belay-noise. I left out 6 pairs whose two seeds differ by 0.03–0.21 on the macro and by as much on Uncheatable (broken or diverged runs). Kept in, they swamp the overall variance, but the near-frontier numbers above barely move: for example, the gain is 1.38× instead of 1.48×.

comments.author: Helw150
comments.body:
**Try numerically stable cross-entropy from [arXiv:2610.31642](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.31642).**

The paper identifies a numerical problem with standard softmax cross-entropy called **Softmax Collapse**. When the correct logit becomes sufficiently larger than the others, floating-point rounding makes its softmax probability exactly 1, zeroing its gradient while leaving non-target gradients nonzero. This breaks the zero-sum gradient invariant (the gradients across all logits should sum to zero) and can cause optimization instability, including sudden spikes in training loss.

The proposed fix is simple: exclude the correct class from the log-sum-exp calculation and use `softplus` to combine the result with the correct class's logit.

```python
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp

def cross_entropy(logits, targets):
    target_logits = jnp.take_along_axis(
        logits, targets[..., None], axis=-1
    )
    is_target = jax.nn.one_hot(
        targets, logits.shape[-1], dtype=jnp.bool_
    )

    others = jnp.where(is_target, -jnp.inf, logits - target_logits)
    return jax.nn.softplus(
        jax.scipy.special.logsumexp(others, axis=-1)
    )
```

This is mathematically equivalent to standard cross-entropy but avoids prematurely zeroing small gradients.

comments.author: armorfaye
comments.body:
Try replacing top-k routing with ReMoE’s ReLU routing and adaptive, load-aware sparsity regularization. Target the same average number of active experts as the baseline, while allowing the count to vary across tokens. Use the paper’s unnormalized nonnegative routing weights.

Rationale: expert selection becomes continuous as routing weights cross zero, and different tokens can receive different amounts of computation. ReMoe (https://arxiv.org/html/2412.14711v2) reports improved language-model loss across several scales. Track active-expert counts and load imbalance, and include the initially denser training phase in the fixed-time comparison.

comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
**Try adding CPLM Plus from #10678 to the Belay experiment ladder.** It extends the copy head with predecessor-conditioned keys and normalized case-class emissions, adding only d² + 2d + 1 parameters over ordinary CPLM.

The archived seed-0 TPU results look promising: Paloma / Uncheatable macro BPB improves from 1.184407 / 0.960857 to 1.181649 / 0.953552 at d512, and from 1.093305 / 0.853946 to 1.091306 / 0.850160 at d768, compared with ordinary CPLM. At d1024, Plus also improves over Belay (1.021640 → 1.014601 Paloma; 0.772050 → 0.767052 Uncheatable).

These runs approximately match analytical useful FLOPs, not wall time, and use one seed, so I think this is worth testing against the current recipe under Belay's fixed-time evaluation with paired seeds. The PR is stacked on #10260 and includes the implementation and results; throughput for the current PR revision still needs validation.

comments.author: TimS-ml
comments.body:
Try causal token-level capacity routing in front of the MoE (Mixture-of-Depths style ([arXiv 2404.02258](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.02258)) ), keeping top-k + QB for expert choice.

Following @ClassicLarry's [comment 1](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-6411175364) and  [comment 2](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5862159670) that dynamic compute likely matters more at scale.

Each MoE sublayer gets a small per-token router score. Tokens above a learned threshold go through the routed experts with a larger top-k; the rest go through the shared expert and the residual only. For routed tokens, expert ranking stays as in the current recipe (QB-adjusted logits, same combine weights); only k changes. Mean active experts per token matches the current recipe, e.g. with today's k = 10: 80% of tokens routed at k = 12 or 13, so the average stays ≈ 10.

Rationale: X0220 ([batch](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-6409675987)) showed ReMoE's failure came from the ReLU gates themselves: dead experts (40–278 per layer), 3–8% drops and load imbalance. Its allocation was already adaptive (easiest loss decile ≈ 7.4 experts, rest ≈ 12). This proposal keeps that adaptive allocation but separates the two decisions: *which tokens get more compute* (new router) and *which experts serve them* (top-k + QB, already stable here), so no expert can die from a zero gate. Mixture-of-Depths uses the same capacity idea for whole blocks.

FYI: the original MoD picks the top-k tokens over the whole sequence during training, so whether position t is routed depends on later tokens. Use a causal version instead: each token is routed by comparing its own score to a learned threshold (or a running causal quantile), with the same rule in training and eval.

comments.author: TimS-ml
comments.body:
Revisit MTP as a low-weight, decaying auxiliary loss computed on a subset of positions, with a block-head variant.

Batch 18 ([comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5843750617)) tried one MTP configuration: a depth-1 head (h_t + W·norm(embed(t+1)) through the shared lm_head), weight 0.3 for the whole run. 

Rationale: MTP results in the literature come from much longer token budgets, so an equal-steps vs fixed-time pair on this ladder says whether the Batch 18 loss came from the configuration or from the objective at this budget. 

Here are some things worth trying:
1. **Lower weight:** 0.05 and 0.1 instead of 0.3.
2. **Decay to zero:** linearly to 0 by 50% or 80% of training, so the late phase optimizes next-token loss only. One extra arm turns MTP off entirely after the first 50%.
3. **Block head:** replace the linear head with one lightweight Transformer block (local attention + dense FFN) that reads norm(h_t) and norm(embed(t+1)) and feeds the shared lm_head, as in DeepSeek-V3 ([arXiv 2412.19437](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.19437)). 
Also, in a recent interview ([video, ~1:30:00](https://youtu.be/V9eI-t3TApE?t=5396)), MiMo-V2.6 leader Fuli Luo said they added MTP in pre-training because it improves the base model, and only later, while designing inference for their hybrid-SWA model, found enough spare decode compute to use MTP for speculative decoding. She also said teams that put too much faith in MLA missed this path; my reading is that MLA leaves less spare decode compute for MTP drafting. That is an inference-side hypothesis without published measurements, and I am not sure if this (spare compute) applies to our situation.
4. **(optional) Subsampled positions:** compute the t+2 logits and loss on a random 25% of positions per batch, still through the shared lm_head. If the cost scales with scored positions, the slowdown drops to about a quarter of 8.6%.

comments.author: armorfaye
comments.body:
Try adding **spelling-normalised byte embeddings** to the input. Each token's input embedding row gets a learned sum over the first 8 UTF-8 bytes of its surface string, one 256 x d table per byte position. Read the bytes after stripping leading spaces and lowercasing, so " The", "the" and "The" share every byte row. Add two small feature rows to keep what the normalisation removes: leading space (0/1) and case (lower, capitalised, all caps, mixed). Zero-init the tables so the model starts identical to the baseline. Add the byte sum to the vocab table before the token gather, so there is no per-token cost and no extra communication. Input side only: do not share byte rows on the lm_head. Keep 8 byte positions and table width d_model at every rung.

Rationale: tokens that are spelling or case variants of each other start with unrelated embeddings and have to learn their similarity from context. Sharing byte rows gives the model that information directly, and it is information the body cannot compute from token ids. This is close to Spelling Bee Embeddings (https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.18030); the space/case normalisation is the addition.

comments.body:

Follow-up to X0226: give the byte features their own AttnRes source instead of adding them to the token embedding. Keep X0226's features as they are (8 spelling-normalised byte positions plus the leading-space and case rows), but gather them from a separate [V, d] table, apply their own RMS norm with its own gain, and add the result to AttnRes as one extra source next to the token embedding. Every Block AttnRes mix and the final readout can then weight spelling and token identity separately. Initialise the byte table like the token embedding, not at zero (the RMS norm of a zero row has an unbounded gradient at step 0). Everything else is unchanged.

comments.author: armorfaye
comments.body:
Track: speedrun

Character n-gram spelling as its own AttnRes source. For each vocabulary token, normalise its string as in X0226 (strip leading spaces, lowercase), add word-boundary markers, and take the set of character 1–4-grams, keeping only n-grams that occur in at least 2 vocabulary tokens. Add X0226's leading-space and case rows. Precompute the [V, K] n-gram index from the tokenizer once. Each token's feature is the sum of its n-gram rows from one learned table, initialised like the token embedding. Apply its own RMS norm with its own gain, and add the result to AttnRes as one extra source next to the token embedding rather than summing it into the token row. With the 16k tokenizer this is about 15k table rows and no extra matmul FLOPs. Use no positional byte features.

comments.body:

Lift the lm_head rank above d_model with bilinear features of the final hidden state. From the final-normed hidden state h, compute f = g ⊙ rms_norm((h A) ⊙ (h B)). A and B are [d, d/4], optimised like the other dense matrices, and g is a zero-init [d/4] gain. Feed [h, f] to an lm_head widened by d/4 input rows, with the new rows optimised like the existing head. The soft cap, z-loss and fused CE apply to the widened head unchanged.

comments.author: xTimeCrystal
comments.body: Track: speedrun Similar to https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.08888, try implementing a Full Bandwidth Transformer (FBT): the trunk runs K parallel passes over the sequence, and pass p's input at token t is fused from that token's embedding and the previous pass's output at token t-1: `x^{(p)}_{t} = norm(x_t + W_fuse norm(h^{(p-1)}_{t-1}))` - Use this formula, not the paper's. This is more stable. - `x_t` is the pass-1 input of token t (its embedding). - `h^{(p-1)}_{t-1}` is the final layer's output of pass `p-1` at position `t-1` (what the LM head reads), not that pass's input. - `norm` is parameter-free RMSNorm. - `W_fuse` is a `d_model` x `d_model` matrix, zero-initialised, so training starts as the plain model. - Position 0 and every document start (BOS) get the plain input `x_t`: no feedback across documents. - Gradients flow through all passes; do not detach or no-grad any pass. - Do not add "jitter" unlike the original paper - Training loss: CE of pass 1 + mean CE of the later passes (ignore as we only test K=2 passes). Evaluation: the last pass only. Sweep the fraction of training steps that use K=2 passes, the rest using K=1: 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1.0 (always 2 passes). Never use K=3. Evaluate every run with K=2. Optimise W_fuse with Muon first, at the learning rate and schedule of the other weight matrices. Then sweep 0.7x and 1.4x to bracket the optimal W_fuse lr using Muon. Then repeat the best Muon run with Adam on `W_fuse` (no weight decay), sweeping its learning rate over 0.7x, 1x, 1.4x. With MoE: keep the expert selections different across passes (the router picks again in every pass; never reuse pass 1's experts—we want the model's second pass picks to be adapted to the "enriched" hidden states). Quantile balancing counts the routing margins of all passes of a batch and updates the bias once, after the batch, for the next batch, never per pass: a per-pass update routes pass 2 with a bias computed from the same batch's own tokens, including later positions, which breaks causality. Compare against the dense baseline at matched training FLOPs: K=2 costs about 2x the FLOPs per token. Also, confirm that sequential decoding (token by token, each token fused with the previous token's final state) gives the same hidden-state and loss (within noise) as K=2 parallel passes. In our nanochat run they agreed to within 0.0003 bpb. nanochat results (per-iteration val bpb using the last pass; fbt2 = always 2 passes): This image shows the untuned baseline; it does not quite break even for the extra compute, and more tuning could close that gap.

comments.author: armorfaye
comments.body:

Track: speedrun

Exact-match pointer mixture on the output with 8 candidates. For every position t, collect K = 8 candidate next tokens from earlier in the same document: for n = 1 and n = 2, the tokens that followed the 4 most recent earlier positions s < t whose last n tokens equal the n tokens ending at t (candidate x[s+1]). Mix them into the output: p(y) = (1 - G) p_vocab(y) + open * sum_k pi_k [c_k = y], where (pi_0, pi_1..pi_K) = softmax(0, l_1..l_K) over the candidates that exist, l_k = h . w_k + 8 * b[k, a_k] - 2 with h the lm_head input and a_k the number of other slots proposing the same token, G = open * sum_k pi_k, open = clip(8 * o, 0, 1). w [d_model, 8], b [8, 8] and the scalar o are zero-initialised and trained in the plain Adam group with no weight decay, so the model starts as the control. Train and evaluate on the mixture loss ce - log((1 - G) + M exp(ce)), where ce is the lm_head's per-token cross-entropy (plus z-loss in training) and M the pointer mass on the label. Implementation: find the matches with integer work on the token ids only, per sequence: sort (document id, key, position) with key = token for n = 1 and previous_token * vocab + token for n = 2, take the sorted neighbour as the previous match and follow those links three more times for the older matches, then gather x[s+1]; batch the sorts over rows. comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
Track: speedrun

Softcap radial MuonH: give each hidden matrix a learned, bounded radius on top of MuonH's sphere.

(Generated by an automated research harness; reasoning and evidence below.)

**Update rule (per Muon-group matrix slice W)**
- Write W = r0 · exp(s) · Ŵ, where r0 is the init radius and Ŵ is on the unit Frobenius sphere. Ŵ takes the usual MuonH hyperball step.
- s (a scalar log-radius per slice) is stepped by Adam on the radial gradient g = <∂L/∂W, W>, at the same LR and schedule as the matrix LR (radius-LR multiplier 1).
- Bound: outward steps are scaled by (1 − (s/c)²) and inward steps are taken in full, so s never passes c. With c = 2, the radius is capped at e² ≈ 7.4× init. When the pull reverses, s comes back immediately.
- Slices whose output passes through a scale-removing norm keep a fixed radius, i.e. plain MuonH. In this recipe that means MLA q/k under the q/k norms, and the KV/latent down-projections. Their radial gradient is zero by Euler's theorem, so learning a radius there only accumulates rounding drift.
- Head and fallback groups are unchanged (AdamH head, Adam fallbacks).

**How it scales (no per-size constant)**
- The radius LR is the rung's MuonH LR from MoeHeuristic, so it moves with the heuristic.
- c = 2 at every rung. At d768 the result is flat for caps from 2.5× to 15× (15× is within 0.0003 of 7.4×), and only a 1.5× cap loses the gain.
- The frozen set is defined by role (followed by a normalization), so it is the same rule at every width.

**Evidence so far (not on the Belay recipe)**
This was measured on a different MoE recipe: d768, 384 experts, KDA + MLA with qk_norm off, batch 128, ctx 4096, 6930 steps, Paloma validation CE.
- Seeds 0-1 mean: softcap 2.5060, MuonH 2.5229, MuonW (lr 1, wd 0.1) 2.5156, MuonW tuned on LR × decay (lr 1.41×, wd 0.05) 2.5111.
- Paired against MuonW (lr 1, wd 0.1) on seeds 2-7 (separate from the seeds used to pick the setting): mean −0.0091, one-sided 95% upper bound −0.0056. On a fixed held-out set: −0.0119.
- The paired test against the tuned MuonW on seeds 2-7 is still running. On seeds 0-1 the gap to tuned MuonW is about −0.005.
- Per-family radii stay finite and under the cap (max |log r| ≈ 1.65). Late drift is no larger than MuonW's own norm drift in the same families.

**Mechanism**
MuonH holds the function-relevant matrices at their init radius, but they need to grow about 2.5-5× in the first few hundred steps. Learning the radius only for the first 500 steps and then freezing it keeps nearly all of the gain.

**Caveat for Belay**
About 44% of the d768 gain came from global-attention temperature (MLA q/k growing with qk_norm off). Belay's recipe RMS-norms MLA q/k with qk_mult fixed at 1.3, so that part may not transfer. learnable_qk_mult may recover some of it. Expect a smaller effect than at d768.

**d512 speedrun**
Not available yet. We are running the 8-minute d512 speedrun ourselves against same-commit controls (seeds 0-2, plus the learnable_qk_mult 2×2), and will post the per-seed Paloma macro loss and paired difference here when it finishes.

comments.author: armorfaye
comments.body:
🤖 Posted on behalf of @armorfaye.

Track: speedrun

Document n-gram count cache mixed into the output. For each position t with label y, count over earlier positions s < t of the same packed document: c1 = number of s with x_s = x_t, n1 = number of those with x_{s+1} = y, c2 = number of s with (x_{s-1}, x_s) = (x_{t-1}, x_t) and n2 = number of those with x_{s+1} = y. Let q1 = n1 / c1 and q2 = n2 / c2 (each is a distribution over the vocabulary). Gate logits l_n = h . w_n + 8 * b_n * log2(1 + c_n) / 12 - 2 for n = 1, 2, where h is the lm_head input; (pi_0, pi_1, pi_2) = softmax(0, l_1, l_2) over the orders with c_n > 0; open = clip(8 * o, 0, 1); G = open * (pi_1 + pi_2). The model's distribution is p(y) = (1 - G) * p_vocab(y) + open * (pi_1 * q1(y) + pi_2 * q2(y)). w [d_model, 2], b [2] and the scalar o are zero-initialised and trained in the plain Adam group with no weight decay, so the model starts as the control. Train and evaluate on the mixture loss ce - log((1 - G) + M * exp(ce)), where ce is the lm_head's per-token cross-entropy (plus z-loss in training) and M = open * (pi_1 * q1(label) + pi_2 * q2(label)). Implementation: all counts are integer work on the token ids, once per step before the forward pass and outside value_and_grad and any jax.checkpoint region. Per sequence, sort three key arrays stably with the position as payload: the token x_u; the pair id x_{u-1} * vocab + x_u; and the triple as two int32 keys (pair id of (x_{u-2}, x_{u-1}), x_u). A pair or triple that would cross a document start gets a key no other position has. In each sorted array a run breaks where the key or the document id changes; an element's rank is its index minus its run start (a cumulative max); scatter the ranks back to positions. Then c1(t) = rank_token[t], c2(t) = rank_pair[t], n1(t) = rank_pair[t + 1] and n2(t) = rank_triple[t + 1]. Take ce from the existing fused cross-entropy kernel with per-token reduction; no second pass over the vocabulary, no [batch, seq, vocab] tensor, no lm_head row gather. Target step time within 1% of the control. Same settings at every rung.

comments.author: armorfaye
comments.body:
🤖 Posted on behalf of @armorfaye.

Track: speedrun

MuonC: replace MuonH's hyperball step with Muon plus AdamC-corrected weight decay (Defazio 2025, arXiv 2506.02285, which scales the decay by lr_t^2 / lr_max) for every matrix in the MuonH group. For each MuonH sphere slice W (the slices MuonH already uses: each 2-D matrix, or each leading index of a stacked leaf), store r0 = ||W||_F at init. Each step, take U = O / ||O||_F, where O is the Newton-Schulz output MuonH already computes, and update W <- W - lr_t * r0 * U - (lr_t^2 / lr_max) * lambda * W, with no projection back to the sphere. lr_t is the current MuonH learning rate from the existing schedule and lr_max is its peak. Set lambda = lr_max / 2: for independent steps this makes the init radius the steady state, and the model starts as the control. The KDA write-strength group, lm_head and output_proj (AdamH) and the Adam group are unchanged. There are no new parameters (r0 is one stored scalar per slice). If a second arm fits, run lambda = 5 * lr_max / 2. Target step time within 1% of the control. At every rung, lambda is taken from that rung's own lr_max.

spillover_issues.author: penfever
spillover_issues.body:
Large NCCL MIN/MAX reductions return incorrect values in the initialized SkyRL policy runtime and make strict replica verification reject matching weights.

Reproduce:
1. Initialize the production Ray policy workers on 64 GB200s in one NVLink domain, with PP2/CP4/EP4/DP8, NCCL 2.30.7 and `NCCL_BUFFSIZE=262144`. Retain the actual Megatron data-parallel groups including context parallelism: 32 ranks per pipeline stage.
2. Inside each worker, run this known-input check on its existing group before weight publication:

Pinned inputs: diagnostic revision `767592680758e3bc47c5ecda385973c3199ca033`, frozen configuration SHA256 `0d4ca250683aaa64d295c4137677709b00941ad8ff307055afdf7e5b63e5a2ce`, and the same adopted Snowball SFT export (input artifact version `2026.11.17.1`, identity suffix `81b4d4d5`). Task image: `ghcr.io/marin-community/iris-task@sha256:13519c59442bd70ed5ec2902869f15094992d6849d7e34e353f1338dec7ff5f8`, frozen `megatron production` bootstrap. The Linux runtime manifest pins PyTorch 2.14.1; the loaded PyTorch version was not independently captured in these receipts.

```python
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
import megatron.core.parallel_state as mpu

group = mpu.get_data_parallel_group(with_context_parallel=True)
members = dist.get_process_group_ranks(group)
base = torch.arange(16_777_216, device="cuda", dtype=torch.int32) % 128
source = base + dist.get_rank()
low, high = source.clone(), source.clone()
dist.all_reduce(low, op=dist.ReduceOp.MIN, group=group)
dist.all_reduce(high, op=dist.ReduceOp.MAX, group=group)
assert torch.equal(low, base + min(members))
assert torch.equal(high, base + max(members))
```

Expected: exact integer MIN/MAX values on every member, with source bytes unchanged.

Observed: all 64 workers fail on 64 MiB arrays in their two 32-rank dense groups. Rank 0 has 11,620,913 wrong MIN elements and 11,652,720 wrong MAX elements. The same handles pass at 1,024 and 4,194,305 elements. The eight-rank expert groups pass all three sizes. Independent NumPy hashes confirm the results; all 128 failed output hashes differ from every possible rank-offset reference pattern, which excludes a simple wrong-member set as the explanation.

At the strict comparator boundary, all 117,568 live sender tensors retain their entry/exit hashes, data/storage pointers, offsets, strides and tensor IDs. Actual group names and members match the expected geometry. Replica hashes agree, source intervals do not overlap, and input bytes stay unchanged during the known-input reductions. The unchanged `compare_replicas` then reports 876,550,056–945,509,596 mismatched bytes per rank. Its current 16 MiB raw-byte chunks create 64 MiB int32 reduction buffers: [comparison code on main](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3e8c7baa26a451b1f8c630bd6dc68a7135907a32/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/weight_sync/expert_block/verify_weights.py#L91).

A separate eight-GPU control passes Ray/torchrun, masked/unmasked GPU visibility and `NCCL_BUFFSIZE` unset/262144. This report therefore reproduces the defect inside the initialized 64-worker runtime; an equivalent standalone 32-worker reproduction and the exact NCCL/PyTorch mechanism remain unproven.

Proposed mitigation, not implemented or GPU-qualified: bound raw-byte comparison chunks to 4 MiB so each int32 reduction is 16 MiB, while comparing every byte with the same strict MIN/MAX rule. Keep the failing 64 MiB case as a correctness regression and investigate the runtime cause separately.

Pinned analysis and all 516 raw-receipt SHA256 values: `s3://marin-us-east-08a/marin/experiments/nccl-minmax-32-rank-20261118/analysis-v1.json` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-08a%2Fmarin%2Fexperiments%2Fnccl-minmax-32-rank-20261118%2Fanalysis-v1.json)). Diagnostic source revision: `767592680758e3bc47c5ecda385973c3199ca033` (local research commit, not yet published). No fix commit or further GPU iteration has been made.

🤖 Root-cause investigation resumed; the comparison-chunk workaround remains on hold.

Preserved logs from the passing torchrun control and failing full-Ray control both identify **PyTorch 2.14.1+cu132 and NCCL 2.30.7+cuda13.3**. The Ray runtime-env overlays explicitly set `NCCL_CUMEM_ENABLE=0`, `NCCL_BUFFSIZE=262144` and `CUDA_DEVICE_MAX_CONNECTIONS=1`. Those overrides are absent from the torchrun launch command; its full inherited process environment was not captured. Missing overlay or log entries do not establish effective defaults. `NCCL_ALGO`, `NCCL_PROTO`, `NCCL_NVLS_ENABLE` and `NCCL_COLLNET_ENABLE` are absent from the preserved Ray overlays, and WARN-level policy logs do not identify the selected algorithm/protocol.

The original three-rack runtime also explicitly set `NCCL_NET=IB`, `NCCL_IB_DISABLE=0`, `NCCL_IB_HCA=ibp` and `NCCL_SOCKET_FAMILY=AF_INET`. The later full-Ray control reproduces the failure without those explicit overrides. These are observed overlays, not proof of which transport each communicator selected.

The original three-rack traceback stops in `_sync_policy_for_rollouts(reason="initial")`. The frozen source places that await before rollout collection and learner forward/backward, so no gradient-training reduction executed. Initialization/publication collectives did execute. Its recipe requests FP32 gradient reduction and averaging inside collectives; their correctness on large buffers remains unestablished.

A **32-GB200, one-NVLink-domain probe** is submitted at production priority, capped at 15 minutes / 8 GB200-hours. It compares fresh Ray and torchrun workers with the three settings unset versus `0/262144/1`, retaining a production WARN baseline and a separate TRACE duplicate. It bisects message size and communicator size/placement, tests 64 MiB FP32/BF16 SUM and AVG, and records effective process NCCL environment/config files, loaded library hashes and bounded traces. BF16 test patterns keep every intermediate integer sum below 256 to avoid rounding ambiguity. Numerical failures intentionally fail the root only after the matrix completes; `receipt.completed` distinguishes that outcome from a harness error.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
🤖 Probe .24 isolates an interaction between CuMem disabled and a 256-KiB SIMPLE buffer on this NVL72 topology. Neither setting alone reproduces the corruption.

Independent NumPy reconstruction verifies 352 completed rank reports and 9,504 known input/output hash checks from eleven profiles. All 32 ranks fail the production profile and the same profile with CUDA_DEVICE_MAX_CONNECTIONS unset. Every rank passes each setting alone, the production profile with CUMEM_ENABLE or BUFFSIZE unset, and production with NVLS disabled, Ring forced or Tree forced. Thus MAX_CONNECTIONS=1 is not required; CUMEM_ENABLE=0 plus BUFFSIZE=262144 and the selected NVLS path reproduce the failure. This does not establish behavior on other hardware or NCCL versions.

Traces show a change in NCCL’s logical topology on the same physical NVLink fabric: with CuMem disabled, NCCL reports MNNVL=0, eight nodes/four local ranks, and cross-host NET/IB/GDRDMA. With CuMem unset, it reports MNNVL=1, one domain/32 local ranks. The passing .14 policy had nccl_buffer_size_bytes=null; failing .15 set 262144 in the three-rack profile (introduced in 76aa8cc2b3, experiments/post_training/long_loop/nvl72.py:126). The change was therefore not only replica-group size or rack count.

The final twelfth .24 profile did not complete: forcing NVLSTree while MNNVL combines the GPUs into one node fails with `No algorithm/protocol available for function AllReduce with datatype ncclInt32`. This is an unavailable algorithm control, not a numerical pass/fail. All eleven prior profiles completed on all ranks; their receipts and all 384 rank-log hashes were verified. The root exited on that last error, so do not describe .24 as a completed twelve-profile matrix.

A source-based mechanism remains to be tested: NCCL v2.30.7-1 src/enqueue.cc:2276 replaces the NVLSTree chunk with its tuning value without capping it to buffSizes[SIMPLE]/NCCL_STEPS. The preserved tuning permits 64/128 KiB payloads while the 256 KiB buffer has 32 KiB slots (eight steps). Device primitives address FIFO slots by connection step size. The exact public-source-to-loaded-wheel build match is not established; this is a hypothesis, not a proved implementation defect.

Submitted `/benfeuer/mochi-nccl-mechanism-20261118-25` at 09:30:27 UTC, source `cbf52ee2d97e72df0f08c911aa6dd1220375e792`. Eight GB200 across two four-GPU hosts in one NVLink domain, production priority, 15 min / ≤2 GB200-hours, zero retries. Six fresh-process variants hold CuMem disabled and NVLSTree fixed, sweeping buffers of 256 KiB, 512 KiB, 1 MiB and 4 MiB, then 256 KiB with NCCL_NVLSTREE_MAX_CHUNKSIZE at 32/64 KiB. Exact 16/32/64 MiB int32 MIN/MAX/SUM and 64 MiB FP32/BF16 SUM retain the failing-size checks. AVG is not run under forced NVLSTree. If the eight-rank positive control does not reproduce, retain that limitation and compare the positive control with the capacity/payload controls at 32 ranks. No production recipe or comparator chunk changes; Exp3 .55 remains untouched.

.24 cost 2.305422 controller-duration GB200-hours; cumulative .16–.24 is 26.300022, not provider billing. Analysis was published and read back exactly: s3://marin-us-east-08a/marin/experiments/nccl-minmax-32-rank-20261118/mechanism24/independent-analysis-v1.json ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-08a%2Fmarin%2Fexperiments%2Fnccl-minmax-32-rank-20261118%2Fmechanism24%2Findependent-analysis-v1.json)). Exact int32 and FP32 MIN/MAX/SUM cover 16/32/64 MiB. Receipts pin environment, library, group membership, input/output hashes, GPU UUIDs, timings and traces. Task wrappers upload all per-node reports before a final CPU Gloo barrier and root verdict. This tests whether the failure reproduces without ProcessGroupNCCL or communicator splitting; results remain pending. Twenty-five focused tests, the two-process CPU oracle and required lint/type checks pass; the direct NCCL API still requires this GPU qualification. comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
🤖 The .25 FIFO-capacity sweep matches the source-predicted boundary on all eight GPUs. `receipt.completed=true`: all six profiles completed; the root then intentionally rejected numerical errors.

Independent NumPy reconstruction verifies all 48 rank reports, 1,008 input/output hash checks and all 48 log hashes. Every rank-0 reduction trace selects NVLS_TREE/SIMPLE throughout the sweep. CuMem disabled, MAX_CONNECTIONS=1 and the algorithm are fixed; neither Ray nor model weights are involved.

| Buffer / per-step slot | 16 MiB int32 MIN/MAX/SUM | 32 MiB | 64 MiB and FP32/BF16 SUM |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 256 KiB / 32 KiB | fail | fail | fail |
| 512 KiB / 64 KiB | pass | pass | fail |
| 1 MiB / 128 KiB | pass | pass | pass |
| 4 MiB / 512 KiB | pass | pass | pass |
| 256 KiB / 32 KiB, NVLSTree payload cap 32 KiB | pass | pass | pass |
| 256 KiB / 32 KiB, NVLSTree payload cap 64 KiB | fail | fail | fail |

Each cell has the same verdict on all eight ranks. These results support the FIFO-slot-overlap mechanism: the host NVLSTree payload selection can exceed a SIMPLE connection slot. The public v2.30.7-1 source initializes the slot from buffSizes[SIMPLE]/NCCL_STEPS, then its NVLS_TREE branch replaces the payload with the independently tuned NVLS size without that bound. Device connection offsets still advance by the connection step size. The source-derived payloads are 64 KiB for the 16/32-MiB cases and 128 KiB for 64 MiB on this geometry, matching the observed staircase. Library SHA remains fc7ea66334edbc934aa25959b9907dbb2b91a1d2485beff18839afc45cbc08d0.

A general production fix is not yet qualified. Passing 64 MiB at 1-MiB buffer capacity does not establish safety for larger payloads or other geometries. The exact public-source-to-wheel build match is not established. Direct-NCCL probe .26 is pending to check whether the failure also occurs without ProcessGroupNCCL or communicator splitting. No application comparator chunking or production settings changed; Exp3 .55 remains untouched.

.25 used 0.348667 controller-duration GB200-hours; cumulative .16–.25 is 26.648689, not provider billing. All tasks released. Verified analysis: s3://marin-us-east-08a/marin/experiments/nccl-minmax-32-rank-20261118/mechanism25/independent-analysis-v1.json ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-08a%2Fmarin%2Fexperiments%2Fnccl-minmax-32-rank-20261118%2Fmechanism25%2Findependent-analysis-v1.json)).
